001.name: Vendetta
001.meaning: Killing the killer of a senior relative, after filing notice with the authorities.
001.hitokoto: Avenging a parent became a crime with a single proclamation, on 7 February 1873.
body: Revenge in the Edo period was not an unchecked private feud but a licensed institution with a procedure set by the shogunate. A samurai obtained a licence from his lord, filed notice with the magistrate's office, and could set out after his enemy only once the entry stood in the town magistrate's revenge register. It applied only when a senior relative such as a father, mother or elder brother had been killed. Killing the avenger in self-defence was lawful, and juteki, a second round of revenge by that side, was forbidden. An unreported revenge killing was investigated, and punished as murder if it was not recognised as revenge.

The Meiji government at first carried the arrangement over in the Provisional Penal Code of 1868. Then, on 7 February 1873, Grand Council Proclamation No. 37, "Revenge Is Strictly Forbidden", was issued at the initiative of Justice Minister Shinpei Eto. Punishing those who kill is "the public authority of the government"; revenge is "an offence against public authority in the name of private duty". Bereaved kin were ordered from then on to "report to the authorities". The revenge clauses left the statute books entirely only with the Penal Code of 1880.

Seven years after the proclamation, on 17 December 1880, Rokuro Usui, a former retainer of the Akizuki domain, killed his father's enemy Naohisa Ichinose in Tokyo. On 22 September 1881 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for premeditated murder. An act that in Edo would have been entered in the register and praised was tried as murder in the same country. The licensed institution thus ended with a date attached.

made.label: Early-modern Licensed on notice
made.fact: Under the Tokugawa shogunate a procedure took hold: a samurai obtained a licence from his lord, filed notice with the magistrate's office, and pursued his enemy only after the entry was made in the town magistrate's revenge register and a copy issued. It applied only when a senior relative such as a father, mother or elder brother had been killed. Killing the avenger in self-defence was lawful; a second round of revenge by that side (juteki) was forbidden. An unreported revenge killing was investigated, and punished as murder if it was not recognised as revenge.

discontinued.label: 1873 Revenge strictly forbidden
discontinued.fact: 7 February 1873 (Meiji 6): Grand Council Proclamation No. 37, "Revenge Is Strictly Forbidden". Punishing those who kill is "the public authority of the government"; revenge is "an offence against public authority in the name of private duty" and was strictly forbidden. Bereaved kin were ordered instead to "set out the facts in full and report them promptly to the authorities".

keyfacts.text: On 7 February 1873, Grand Council Proclamation No. 37, "Revenge Is Strictly Forbidden", was promulgated. It forbade revenge as "an offence against public authority in the name of private duty" and ordered bereaved kin to report to "the authorities".

The proclamation was drafted on the strong initiative of Justice Minister Shinpei Eto. The new Meiji government had licensed revenge as before in the Provisional Penal Code of 1868, and the revenge clauses left the statute books entirely only with the Penal Code of 1880 (Meiji 13).

In the Edo period, revenge by a samurai required a licence from his lord and notice to the magistrate's office; the entry was made in the town magistrate's revenge register and a copy issued. Revenge without permission was investigated and punished as murder if it was not recognised as revenge. It applied only to senior relatives such as a father, mother or elder brother, and juteki, revenge taken in turn against the avenger, was forbidden.

On 17 December 1880, Rokuro Usui, a former retainer of the Akizuki domain, killed his father's enemy Naohisa Ichinose at the Tokyo residence of his former lord Kuroda. On 22 September 1881 the Tokyo Court sentenced him to life imprisonment in the form reserved for the privileged classes. The amnesty on the promulgation of the Constitution in 1889 reduced it to ten years' confinement, and he left prison on 22 September 1891.
In the Kogi on-cho register of the Edo town magistrate's office, ordinary revenge killings decline from the Genroku era (1688-1703) onward.

002.name: Loyalty & Filial Piety
002.hitokoto: Handed to every school in 1890; both houses recalled it on 19 June 1948.
body: Teaching loyalty and filial piety together to ordinary people begins in early-modern times. In 1722 the shogunate had Muro Kyuso translate a Ming book of precepts, printed Rikuyu engi taii officially and spread it as a text in the terakoya schools. In 1801 it gathered and published the commendations of 8,610 filial children and others, reported from across the country, as Kankoku kogiroku. Loyalty and filial piety were virtues the shogunate distributed and rewarded.

The Imperial Rescript on Education of 30 October 1890 opened "Our subjects, being loyal, being filial, millions of hearts as one, have through the ages made this beauty complete", and placed loyalty and filial piety as "the glory of the national polity" and "the source of education". In the form of the imperial name and seal alone, without the countersignature of a Minister of State, it was read aloud on school ceremonial days and made standard equipment for every citizen as the root norm of moral training.

After the defeat, the Ministry of Education removed the requirement to read it aloud by ministerial ordinance in 1946, but the decisive discontinuation is 19 June 1948. On that day the plenary session of the House of Representatives passed the Resolution on the Exclusion of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts, and the plenary session of the House of Councillors the Resolution Confirming the Invalidity of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts, both proposed jointly by all parties. The order of business and the text as read out remain in the record of Diet proceedings.

made.label: 1722 Rikuyu engi taii
made.fact: In 1722 the shogunate had Muro Kyuso render a Ming book of precepts into Japanese as Rikuyu engi taii, printed it officially and spread it as a text for the terakoya schools. In 1801 it recorded and published the commendations of 8,610 filial children and others, reported from across the country, in Kankoku kogiroku. The Imperial Rescript on Education of 30 October 1890 placed "being loyal, being filial" as the glory of the national polity and the source of education.

discontinued.label: 1948 Excluded by the Diet
discontinued.fact: On 19 June 1948 the plenary session of the House of Representatives passed the Resolution on the Exclusion of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts (submitted by Junzo Matsumoto and 34 others, jointly by all parties), and the plenary session of the House of Councillors passed the Resolution Confirming the Invalidity of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts (moved by Kotaro Tanaka and 25 others, jointly by all parties).

keyfacts.text: Promulgated on 30 October 1890, the Imperial Rescript on Education stated "Our subjects, being loyal, being filial, millions of hearts as one, have through the ages made this beauty complete; herein lies the glory of Our national polity, and herein too lies the source of education", placing loyalty and filial piety as the glory of the national polity and the source of education. It runs to 315 characters in all, in the form of the imperial name and seal alone, without the countersignature of a Minister of State.

On 19 June 1948 the plenary session of the House of Representatives took up, without committee examination, the draft Resolution on the Exclusion of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts, submitted by Junzo Matsumoto and 34 others, and passed it. The text states that the fundamental idea of the rescripts rests on "sovereignty residing in the monarch and a mythical view of the national polity".

The same day, the plenary session of the House of Councillors passed, as the second item on the order of business, the draft Resolution Confirming the Invalidity of the Imperial Rescript on Education and Other Rescripts, moved by Kotaro Tanaka and 25 others, confirming that the Imperial Rescript on Education, together with the Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors, the Boshin Rescript and others, "has already been abolished and has lost its effect".

Education Minister Tatsuo Morito explained in the House of Representatives that day that the Ministry of Education had, by ministerial ordinance of 3 March 1946, made void the provision that moral training be conducted on the basis of the purport of the Imperial Rescript on Education, and by ministerial ordinance of 9 October the same year deleted the provision for reading the rescript aloud on ceremonial days.

In 1722 the shogunate had Muro Kyuso translate the Ming work Liuyu yanyi into Japanese as Rikuyu engi taii, printed it officially and used it as a text in popular education such as the terakoya schools (the six maxims are the six articles of the Ming emperor Hongwu: filial obedience to parents, respect for elders and so on).

In 1789 the shogunate ordered reports from across the country of commendations of filial children and others, and 8,600 cases covering 8,610 people were compiled at the Shoheizaka Academy and published in 1801 as Kankoku kogiroku.

003.name: Shudo
003.hitokoto: Some acts between men were punishable under national law for less than ten years.
body: Relations between men of different ages, an older man and a youth not yet through his coming-of-age rite, were open culture in medieval temples and in early-modern samurai society. Ihara Saikaku's The Great Mirror of Male Love (1687) gives 20 of its 40 chapters to shudo among the samurai and the other 20 to the world of the young kabuki actors. It was spoken of as a bond, not a shame.

In the eleventh month of 1872 the Ministry of Justice, answering a query from Shirakawa Prefecture, issued the keikan regulation, and Article 266 of the Revised Criminal Regulations, in force from July 1873, set "90 days' penal labour for whoever commits sodomy". Peers and former samurai, however, were "dealt with as grossly shameless": the article ran differently by status. It was not carried into the Penal Code of 1880 and was gone when that code came into force on 1 January 1882.

What followed the end of the crime was pathology. Popular sexology, such as Hentai seiyokuron of 1915, retold male love as "perversion", and Makoto Furukawa argued that this turn was a change of codes. The American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from the DSM on 15 December 1973; the WHO removed it in ICD-10 on 17 May 1990. In Japan, Shibuya Ward passed its ordinance on 31 March 2015, and the first certificates were issued on 5 November that year.

made.label: 1687 The Great Mirror of Male Love
made.fact: Ihara Saikaku's The Great Mirror of Male Love (published in the fourth month of 1687, 8 volumes, 40 chapters) gives its first 20 chapters to shudo in samurai society and its last 20 to the world of the young kabuki actors. Earlier works exist, such as the chigo tales of the Muromachi period.

discontinued.label: 1873 Criminalised by statute
discontinued.fact: On 13 November 1872 the Ministry of Justice, answering a query from Shirakawa Prefecture, issued the keikan (sodomy) regulation. Article 266 of the Revised Criminal Regulations, in force from July 1873: "Whoever commits sodomy shall each serve 90 days' penal labour; peers and former samurai shall be dealt with as grossly shameless." It was not carried into the Penal Code of 1880 and disappeared when that code came into force on 1 January 1882. Popular sexology then pathologised it as "perversion", as in Hentai seiyokuron of 1915.

keyfacts.text: It began in the ninth month of 1872, when Shirakawa Prefecture (now northern Kumamoto) asked the Ministry of Justice about punishing "male love" in public schools and private academies. The ministry drafted the regulation in a document dated 15 October and issued the keikan regulation on 13 November: "Whoever entices another and commits sodomy shall receive 90 strokes; peers and former samurai shall be dealt with as grossly shameless…"

Article 266 of the Revised Criminal Regulations of 1873 read: "Whoever commits sodomy shall each serve 90 days' penal labour. Peers and former samurai shall be dealt with as grossly shameless. A child of 15 or under who is so used is not liable. Whoever commits rape shall serve ten years' penal labour." It set a different treatment for peers and former samurai: a provision of status law.

The sodomy provision was not included in the Penal Code enacted in 1880, and ceased to exist when that code came into force on 1 January 1882. This is held to be the only period in which some consensual sexual acts between men (keikan) were subject to criminal penalty under national law in Japan.

Hentai seiyokuron by Eiji Habuto and Junjiro Sawada (Shun'yodo, published 15 June 1915, 704 pages) is the representative work of "popular sexology". Furukawa (1994) argued that the turn in discourse on homosexuality in modern Japan was a change of three codes (U.S.-Japan Women's Journal, no. 17, pp.29-55).

The Board of Trustees of the American Psychiatric Association (APA) approved the decision to remove homosexuality from DSM-II on 15 December 1973, and the WHO approved ICD-10 at the 43rd World Health Assembly on 17 May 1990, dropping the classification of homosexuality.

On 31 March 2015 the Shibuya Ward assembly passed an ordinance including certification of same-sex partnerships. On 5 November that year, certificates and acknowledgements were issued to one couple in Shibuya Ward and seven couples in Setagaya Ward. The Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity in Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity was enacted on 16 June 2023 and promulgated and in force on 23 June.

004.name: Inkyo Retirement
004.hitokoto: The Civil Code set inkyo at 60 or over. Its articles went on 1 January 1948.
body: Inkyo in the Edo period was a widely seen life plan: the head passed the headship on while still alive and stepped back from the front line. A samurai petitioned his lord and passed the headship to his son; a townsman left the shop and handed property and rights to his successor. Documents kept in Ranzan, Saitama, from 1802 and 1867 record inkyo-men arrangements, by which the new head promised the retired head an annual allowance of rice, money and fields.

The Meiji Civil Code, in force from 1898, wrote the custom into articles as a legal act with requirements of age and more. Article 752 made inkyo conditional on the house head being 60 full years or more and on the heir to the headship accepting the succession without reservation; Article 964 set inkyo, alongside the death of the house head, as a ground on which succession to the headship began. Notice went to the registrar. Inkyo became an institution whose requirements the state managed.

On 3 May 1947, Article 3 of the Emergency Measures Act, in force with the Constitution, provided that "the provisions on the house head, family members and otherwise concerning the house shall not apply", and the amended Civil Code promulgated on 22 December that year came into force on 1 January 1948, at which point the inkyo articles were gone. What decides the time to step back instead is the mandatory retirement age: in 1968, 69.0% of firms with 30 or more employees had one; in 2022, 94.4%. In March 2020, Quit Like a Millionaire, which argues for early retirement, appeared in Japanese.

made.label: Early-modern The standard life plan
made.fact: A samurai petitioned his lord and passed the headship to his son; a townsman left the shop and passed property and rights to his successor; a farmer handed his fields to his son and retired. Documents kept in Ranzan, Saitama, a bond of 1802 and a note of 1867, record inkyo-men arrangements, by which the new head promised the retired head an annual allowance of rice, money and fields.

discontinued.label: 1948 Abolished by the Civil Code
discontinued.fact: The Act on Emergency Measures concerning the Civil Code Accompanying the Enforcement of the Constitution of Japan (Act No. 74 of 19 April 1947), in force from 3 May 1947, provided in Article 3 that "the provisions on the house head, family members and otherwise concerning the house shall not apply", suspending the inkyo provisions. The Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 222), promulgated on 22 December 1947, came into force on 1 January 1948 and deleted the articles.

restocked.label: 2020 FIRE
restocked.fact: Quit Like a Millionaire by Kristy Shen and Bryce Leung, translated by Masaaki Iwamoto (Diamond, Inc.), was published in Japanese in March 2020 and became a bestseller.

keyfacts.text: Article 752 of the Meiji Civil Code (in force 16 July 1898) provided that a house head could not retire unless he both was "60 full years or more" and had "an heir to the headship with full capacity accepting the succession without reservation"; Article 753 made special retirement for illness and the like subject to the permission of the court. Article 964 gives the grounds on which succession to the headship begins as "the death, retirement or loss of nationality of the house head".

Article 3 of the Emergency Measures Act (Act No. 74 of 1947), promulgated on 19 April and in force from 3 May 1947, provided that "the provisions on the house head, family members and otherwise concerning the house shall not apply". The provisions on inkyo and the house head lost their effect at the same moment the Constitution came into force.

The Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 222 of 1947), promulgated on 22 December 1947, wholly revised the books on relatives and on succession, and its entry into force on 1 January 1948 deleted the articles on succession to the headship and on inkyo.

According to the Survey on Employment Management by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (firms of 30 or more employees), 69.0% of firms had a mandatory retirement age in 1968, when the survey began (about 95% among firms with 300 or more, 51.0% among those with 30 to 99). It passed 90% in 1991. As of 1968, 63.5% of uniform retirement ages were 55 or under.

In the 2022 General Survey on Working Conditions, 94.4% of firms had a mandatory retirement age, and 96.9% of those a uniform one. Under the Act on Stabilization of Employment of Elderly Persons as amended in 1994, a retirement age below 60 became unlawful from April 1998.

The oldest mandatory retirement age in Japan is held to be the 55 in the workers' regulations of the Tokyo Artillery Arsenal in 1887, and in the private sector the 55 in the rules on leave of absence at Nippon Yusen in 1902 (life expectancy for men was then about 43).

005.name: The House Name First
005.hitokoto: The "house" became law on 16 July 1898 and lost its effect on 3 May 1947.
body: The criterion that puts not letting the house name die out above all else had long been rooted in samurai society, but what made it law for every citizen was the books on relatives and on succession of the Meiji Civil Code, in force from 16 July 1898. Article 746: "The house head and the family members bear the surname of the house." Article 750 made the consent of the house head a requirement for a family member's marriage. Article 970 ranked heirs to the headship by male sex, legitimacy and seniority.

The discontinuation came in two stages. On 3 May 1947, Article 3 of the Emergency Measures Act (Act No. 74 of 1947), in force together with the Constitution of Japan, stopped the provisions concerning the house from applying, and the amendment to the Civil Code (Act No. 222) promulgated on 22 December that year came into force on 1 January 1948, at which point the articles on the house head and succession to the headship were gone. The ground for this is Article 24 of the Constitution: individual dignity and the essential equality of the sexes.

The law is gone, but stock with the price tag removed is still on the shelf. Of the 474,741 marriages in 2023, 94.5% chose the husband's surname. Meanwhile reburials, moving the graves of ancestors, rose from 91,567 in fiscal 2015 to 166,886 in fiscal 2023. The apparatus for keeping up the house name is being taken apart, slowly, outside the law.

made.label: 1898 The Meiji Civil Code
made.fact: Books 4 and 5 of the Civil Code (Act No. 9 of 21 June 1898), promulgated on 21 June and in force from 16 July 1898, defined family members in Article 732 as "the relatives of the house head who are in his house, and their spouses", provided in Article 746 that "the house head and the family members bear the surname of the house", required the consent of the house head for a family member's marriage or adoption in Article 750, and in Article 970 ranked heirs to the headship by nearness of degree, male sex, legitimacy and seniority.

discontinued.label: 1948 The house system abolished
discontinued.fact: Article 3 of the Emergency Measures Act (Act No. 74 of 1947), in force from 3 May 1947, suspended the provisions concerning the house, and the entry into force on 1 January 1948 of the Act Partially Amending the Civil Code (Act No. 222), promulgated on 22 December 1947, deleted the provisions on the house head and succession to the headship.

keyfacts.text: Books 4 (Relatives) and 5 (Succession) of the Civil Code were promulgated as Act No. 9 of 21 June 1898, and under the Act on Enforcement of the Civil Code (Act No. 11 of the same year) the whole of them came into force on 16 July 1898.

Meiji Civil Code Article 746: "The house head and the family members bear the surname of the house." Article 749: "A family member may not fix his residence against the will of the house head." Article 750: "A family member who marries or adopts must obtain the consent of the house head." Article 970 ranked heirs to the headship by degree of kinship, male sex, legitimacy and seniority.

Article 3 of the "Act on Emergency Measures concerning the Civil Code Accompanying the Enforcement of the Constitution of Japan" (Act No. 74 of 1947), promulgated on 19 April 1947, provided that "the provisions on the house head, family members and otherwise concerning the house shall not apply". From 3 May, the day the Constitution came into force, the provisions of the house system lost their effect.

The "Act Partially Amending the Civil Code" (Act No. 222 of 1947), promulgated on 22 December 1947, came into force on 1 January 1948, abolishing succession to the headship and providing for the spouse's right of inheritance and for equal shares.
Of the 474,741 marriages in 2023, 448,397 (94.5%) chose the husband's surname and 26,344 (5.5%) the wife's. In 1995 the husband's surname was 97.4%.

The national number of reburials in the Report on Public Health Administration and Services by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare rose from 91,567 in fiscal 2015 to 124,346 in fiscal 2019, 151,076 in fiscal 2022 and 166,886 in fiscal 2023 (these are reburial permits and do not equal the number of graves closed).

006.name: Born to One's Station
006.hitokoto: Samurai status privileges came off over six years, in proclamations from 1870 to 76.
body: Status in early-modern Japan was decided by birth, and the domains entered the stipends and posts of their retainers in a bungen-cho register. Bungen, a word that meant status and property from the late Heian period, gave "know your bun" and "one's station": the norm was to live within that range. Bearing a surname in public and wearing a sword were, as a rule, privileges of the samurai.

The Meiji government undid this not with one statute but with a run of proclamations. Grand Council Proclamation No. 608 of 1870 (19 September Meiji 3) permitted commoners to bear surnames in public; the order of 1871 (9 August Meiji 4) on cropped hair and the removal of swords left hairstyle and the wearing of swords "as one pleases"; on the 23rd of that month came "Marriage Is Permitted Between All from the Peerage Down to Commoners", and on the 28th the so-called Emancipation Edict. Wearing a sword was forbidden by the Sword Abolishment Edict of 28 March 1876 (Grand Council Proclamation No. 38).

The Jinshin household registers of 1872, however, entered the status designations of peers, former samurai and commoners, so the divisions themselves stayed in the register. "Born to one's station" came back under another name in 2021, when oya-gacha, the parent lottery, was chosen for the top ten of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award and took the Daijisen New Word of the Year. What differs from 150 years ago is that it is spoken in the vocabulary of probability rather than of status.

made.label: Early-modern The status order
made.fact: Bungen is a word seen from the late Heian period, meaning social status, rank and property, that is, one's station. In the Edo period the domains entered the names, stipends, ranks and posts of their retainers in a bungen-cho register. Bearing a surname in public and wearing a sword were privileges of the samurai.

discontinued.label: 1871 Sword and hair edicts, etc.
discontinued.fact: Grand Council Proclamation No. 608 of 19 September Meiji 3 (13 October 1870) permitting commoners surnames; Grand Council Order No. 399 of 9 August Meiji 4 (23 September 1871) on cropped hair and the removal of swords; "Marriage Is Permitted Between All from the Peerage Down to Commoners" of 23 August Meiji 4; the so-called Emancipation Edict of 28 August Meiji 4; Grand Council Proclamation No. 38 of 28 March 1876, the Sword Abolishment Edict.

restocked.label: 2021 Parent Gacha
restocked.fact: Oya-gacha was chosen for the top ten of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2021 and took the grand prize in the Daijisen New Word of the Year for the same year. It had been current as the vocabulary of smartphone games from about 2015, and turned into a serious word for inequality from September 2021.

keyfacts.text: On 19 September Meiji 3 (13 October 1870), Grand Council Proclamation No. 608, permitting commoners surnames, allowed commoners to bear a surname in public. Registrations did not proceed, however, and an ordinance making surnames compulsory was to follow in 1875.

On 9 August Meiji 4 (23 September 1871), Grand Council Order No. 399 on cropped hair and the removal of swords provided that "cropped hair, uniform, informal dress and the removal of swords are all to be as one pleases", leaving hairstyle, and the removal of swords other than with formal dress, to each person's own choice.

On 23 August Meiji 4 the Grand Council permitted marriage across status lines, providing that "marriage between all from the peerage down to commoners is permitted; neither side need petition, and notice is to be given to the ward head at the time" (Collection of Laws No. 437). On the 28th of the same month it issued the so-called Emancipation Edict.

Compiled from 1 February Meiji 5 under the Family Register Act of 4 April Meiji 4 (Grand Council Proclamation No. 170), the Jinshin household registers were the first nationally uniform register, replacing the religious census registers, but they kept the status designations of the imperial family, the peerage, the former samurai and commoners as entry items, and so kept the status divisions themselves.

On 28 March 1876, Grand Council Proclamation No. 38, "Wearing a Sword Is Forbidden Except with Court Dress or the Uniform of Soldiers, Police and Officials" (the Sword Abolishment Edict), forbade the wearing of swords.

Bungen is a word from the late Heian period meaning social status, rank and property, one's station, and in the Edo period the daimyo houses compiled a bungen-cho register of their retainers' stipends and posts. Oya-gacha was in the top ten of the 2021 U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award and took the grand prize in the Daijisen New Word of the Year for 2021. The word oya-gacha was first used in the Diet at a plenary session of the House of Councillors on 12 October 2021.

007.name: Impermanence
007.hitokoto: Buddhist meditation on impermanence became a US medical programme in 1979.
body: "The flow of the river never ceases, and yet the water is never the water of before." Hojoki by Kamo no Chomei was completed at the end of the third month of 1212, and The Tale of the Heike appears in a record of 1240 under the name "Jisho monogatari, six volumes, called Heike". In Mujo (1964), Junzo Karaki set out the passage by which the court's hakanashi became mujo in the medieval period and went on to the metaphysics of Dogen. Calling it the operating system of the medieval period is the received view in literary history.

No figures were found, however, to show that it "fell, driven out by the modern view of history as progress". No opinion survey asks about impermanence over time, so the fall remains an interpretation. That Karaki's book was written in 1964 itself shows that impermanence went on being read as a subject after the war. Less a discontinued line than stock with no price tag.

It came back under another name by way of the United States: MBSR, begun by Jon Kabat-Zinn at the University of Massachusetts in 1979, then "Search Inside Yourself", begun inside Google in 2007, and then the NHK Special "Killer Stress" of 18 and 19 June 2016, which introduced mindfulness. The Buddhist observation of impermanence was reimported as a meditation programme.

made.label: 1212 Hojoki
made.fact: Hojoki by Kamo no Chomei was completed at the end of the third month of 1212. The Tale of the Heike is noted in 1240 as "Jisho monogatari, six volumes, called Heike", so it existed by the first half of the 13th century at the latest. Mujo by Junzo Karaki (Chikuma Shobo, 1964) set out the passage from the court's hakanashi to mujo in the medieval period and on to the metaphysics of Dogen.

restocked.label: 2016 Mindfulness
restocked.fact: Jon Kabat-Zinn began MBSR (Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction) at the University of Massachusetts in 1979; the in-house Google course "Search Inside Yourself" began in 2007; and the second part of the NHK Special series "Killer Stress", broadcast on 18 and 19 June 2016, introduced mindfulness as a way of coping.

keyfacts.text: Hojoki was completed by Kamo no Chomei on the last day of the third month of 1212 and begins "The flow of the running river never ceases, and yet the water is not the water of before".

The year The Tale of the Heike was written is unknown, but a record of 1240 speaks of "Jisho monogatari, six volumes, called Heike", and section 226 of Essays in Idleness relates that "Yukinaga, former governor of Shinano, made the Tale of the Heike and taught it to a blind man called Shobutsu to recite".

Mujo by Junzo Karaki (Chikuma Shobo, 1964) is in three parts, hakanashi (the court), mujo (Honen, Shinran, Ippen, Sogi, Basho) and the metaphysics of mujo (Dogen), setting out the changes in the Japanese sense of impermanence.
The in-house Google programme "Search Inside Yourself" was developed in 2007 by the engineer Chade-Meng Tan.

The NHK Special series "Killer Stress" was broadcast on 18 June (part one) and 19 June 2016 (part two), and part two introduced "coping", from cognitive behavioural therapy, and "mindfulness", from meditation, as ways of coping.

In the record of Diet proceedings, "mindfulness" in the sense of meditation appears only once, in an answer by the Director-General of the Correction Bureau of the Ministry of Justice on 14 November 2019; it has not become a word of policy. No statistics or survey were found to show that it "fell, driven out by the modern view of history as progress".

008.name: Mutual Aid Circles
008.hitokoto: Most mujin companies became sogo banks in 1951, and ordinary banks in 1989.
body: Yui, which turned planting and thatching by an exchange of labour, and tanomoshi and mujin, which pooled money and lent it round in turn, were standard equipment of the village community. The word tanomoshi appears in the twelfth month of 1275, in a record of a temple on Mount Koya raising the cost of repairing its bathhouse, written there as hyoshi. It spread among ordinary people in the Muromachi period and settled in by early-modern times as everyday finance.

As an institution, the discontinuation can be dated on the financial side. The Mujin Business Act of 21 June 1915 put mujin run as a business under licence; the Mutual Loan and Savings Bank Act of 5 June 1951 converted mujin companies into sogo banks; on 1 February 1989, 52 sogo banks converted to ordinary banks all at once, and by April 1992 the sogo banks had all gone. The Act itself was repealed in 1992. Yui, for its part, thinned out amid depopulation and mechanisation, leaving no trace in the statistics.

READYFOR began on 29 March 2011 and CAMPFIRE in June of the same year, and the Sharing Economy Association was established in 2016. Gathering small sums from many resembles a tanomoshi-ko, but the line of descent is an import of crowdfunding from the United States, not a direct descendant of the ko. A similar product arrived from a different factory: that is the accurate way to put it.

made.label: 1275 First mention of tanomoshi
made.fact: The word tanomoshi appears in a document of the twelfth month of 1275 from Mount Koya, recording that a temple formed a hyoshi to raise the cost of repairing its bathhouse. It spread among ordinary people in the Muromachi period and settled in in early-modern times. Yui is the joint work of planting, harvesting, thatching a roof and the like by an equal exchange of labour, and the body that organises it.

discontinued.label: 1989 Sogo banks converted
discontinued.fact: The Mujin Business Act (Act No. 24 of 21 June 1915) put mujin run as a business under licence; the Mutual Loan and Savings Bank Act (Act No. 199 of 5 June 1951) converted mujin companies into sogo banks; on 1 February 1989, 52 sogo banks converted to ordinary banks all at once; and the Financial System Reform Act of June 1992 repealed the Mutual Loan and Savings Bank Act.

restocked.label: 2011 Crowdfunding
restocked.fact: READYFOR began service on 29 March 2011, the first purchase-type crowdfunding in Japan, and CAMPFIRE began in June 2011. The Sharing Economy Association announced its founding on 14 December 2015 and was established on 15 January 2016.

keyfacts.text: The first appearance of tanomoshi in writing is a document of the twelfth month of 1275 from Mount Koya, recording that a temple formed a hyoshi to raise funds for repairing its bathhouse. In the Kamakura period it was interest-free, unsecured lending among the poor, but interest and security came in by degrees and it spread widely in the Muromachi period.

Yui is "carrying out joint work by exchanging labour on equal terms, to keep up farming such as planting and harvesting and household life such as housing, or the mutual aid body for that". The rethatching of the gassho roofs of Shirakawa-go was done once every 30 to 40 years by 200 to 300 people in a day. The causes of its decline are depopulation, the decline of primary industry and ageing.
The Mujin Business Act was enacted as Act No. 24 of 21 June 1915 and put mujin run as a business under licence (wholly revised in 1931).

The Mutual Loan and Savings Bank Act was promulgated and came into force as Act No. 199 of 5 June 1951, and encouraged money mujin companies to convert into sogo banks. Sogo banks handled sogo kakekin, instalment savings resembling mujin.

On 1 February 1989, 52 sogo banks across the country converted all at once, with the approval of the Ministry of Finance, into ordinary banks (second-tier regional banks), and the Mutual Loan and Savings Bank Act was repealed by the Financial System Reform Act of June 1992.

READYFOR began service on 29 March 2011 and is held to be the first purchase-type crowdfunding in Japan; CAMPFIRE began in June 2011. The Sharing Economy Association was established on 15 January 2016 (its founding press conference was on 14 December 2015).

009.name: Many Jobs at Once
009.hitokoto: Employees became a majority only in 1959. Before that, self-employment was normal.
body: Early-modern farmers widely took up nokan yogyo, trade and craft work in the farming off season, and in a survey of 1829 covering what is now Yashio, Saitama, about 250 of some 1,000 households were in off-season trade or a craft. In 1843 the shogunate had the off-season livelihoods of the eight Kanto provinces written up. Lower samurai too eked out the household with piecework such as papering umbrellas. In some villages four households in ten had trade or craft work alongside farming.

Working for an employer became the majority only after the war. In the Labour Force Survey the share of employees among all persons in employment was 42.4% in 1953, passed 50% for the first time in 1959, and reached 64.9% in 1970, 77.4% in 1990, 87.3% in 2010 and 90.6% in 2025. On the figures, employment as the majority way of working is a new product of the 1960s onward.

The restocking can be placed in January 2018, when the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare drew up the Guidelines on the Promotion of Side Jobs and Second Jobs, struck the clause "shall not engage in the business of another company without permission" from the Model Rules of Employment, and put in a new clause allowing side jobs. It was a revision of model rules, not of a statute, but in the record of Diet proceedings remarks containing the word fukugyo, side job, rose from 9 in 2013 to 66 in 2018 and 97 in 2024.

made.label: Pre-modern Off-season side work
made.fact: Early-modern farmers ran wage work and trade in the farming off season as nokan yogyo, and in a survey of 1829 covering what is now Yashio, Saitama, about 250 of some 1,000 households were in off-season trade or a craft. In 1843 the shogunate had a Register of Names in Off-Season Livelihoods in the Eight Kanto Provinces compiled. Lower samurai eked out the household with piecework such as papering umbrellas and lanterns.

discontinued.label: 1959 Employees pass half
discontinued.fact: In the Labour Force Survey the share of employees among all persons in employment was 42.4% in 1953 and passed half for the first time in 1959 at 51.9%, reaching 64.9% in 1970, 77.4% in 1990, 87.3% in 2010 and 90.6% in 2025.

restocked.label: 2018 Side-job guidelines
restocked.fact: In January 2018 the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare drew up the Guidelines on the Promotion of Side Jobs and Second Jobs, and at the same time struck "shall not engage in the business of another company without permission" from the Model Rules of Employment and put in a new provision that "a worker may engage in the business of another company outside working hours". The guidelines were revised in September 2020 and July 2022.

keyfacts.text: Share of employees among all persons in employment, from the Labour Force Survey (long-term time series table 4): 42.4% in 1953 (16.60 million employees out of 39.13 million in employment), 51.9% in 1959, 64.9% in 1970, 77.4% in 1990, 87.3% in 2010, 90.6% in 2025 (61.85 million out of 68.28 million). The self-employed went from 9.91 million in 1953 to 4.99 million in 2025, family workers from 12.62 million to 1.15 million.

Early-modern nokan yogyo was wage work and trade carried on by farmers between the tasks of farming; in the off-season survey of 1829, about 250 of some 1,000 households in what is now Yashio were in off-season trade or a craft. In 1843 a Register of Names in Off-Season Livelihoods in the Eight Kanto Provinces was compiled.

Lower samurai and shogunal retainers eked out the household with piecework such as papering umbrellas and lanterns or teaching in a terakoya school, and the Aoyama Hundred-Man Musketeer Corps produced and sold "Aoyama umbrellas" as an organised business.

In January 2018 the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare drew up the Guidelines on the Promotion of Side Jobs and Second Jobs, deleted "shall not engage in the business of another company without permission" from the duties of compliance in the Model Rules of Employment, and put in a new provision on side and second jobs. The guidelines were revised in September 2020 and July 2022.
In the searchable record of Diet proceedings, remarks containing the word fukugyo, side job, rise from 5 in 2010 to 9 in 2013, 30 in 2016, 66 in 2018, 72 in 2021 and 97 in 2024.

010.name: Mottainai
010.hitokoto: Mottainai went out to the world in 2005, in a Kenyan activist's UN speech.
body: Mottainai is used in A Collection of Tales from Uji (c.1221), of the Kamakura period, and mottainashi is listed in the dictionary Gagakushu of 1444. It first meant improper, or too good for one: "mottainaki aruji kana" in Tales from Uji meant "what an improper master". The present use, regretting that a thing is wasted, is already there in The Chronicle of Great Peace in the second half of the 14th century.

The date this word became a world commodity is 4 March 2005. Wangari Maathai, the Kenyan environmental activist who came to Japan that February, learned mottainai from an interview with the Mainichi Shimbun and proposed in a speech at UN headquarters, "let us spread MOTTAINAI to the world". The same day the Mainichi Shimbun set up a secretariat and the campaign began.

The second restocking took the form of a statute. The Act on Promotion of Food Loss and Waste Reduction, promulgated on 31 May 2019 and in force from 1 October, places a duty to reduce food loss on the state, local governments and businesses. A word that in medieval times also meant improper survived as a word for regret at waste, and came back as the MOTTAINAI slogan and as a statute that calls for an awareness of not wasting food.

made.label: c.1221 Tales from Uji
made.fact: Mottainashi is used in A Collection of Tales from Uji (c.1221), of the Kamakura period, and the dictionary Gagakushu, completed in 1444, has entries for mottai and mottainashi in its section on words. Old-language dictionaries give the senses in the order (1) outrageous, improper (Tales from Uji), (2) too good for one, gratifying (the kyogen play Buaku), (3) a shame, a waste, and today almost only the third is used. No primary source was found, within what this catalogue examined, to show when the third sense became the main one.

restocked.label: 2005 MOTTAINAI
restocked.fact: In February 2005 Wangari Maathai (Nobel Peace Prize, 2004), invited to Japan by the Mainichi Shimbun for events marking the entry into force of the Kyoto Protocol, learned the word mottainai, and on 4 March that year proposed at UN headquarters in New York, at the Commission on the Status of Women, "let us spread MOTTAINAI to the world". The same day the Mainichi Shimbun placed a secretariat within the paper and began the MOTTAINAI campaign. The second restocking is the Act on Promotion of Food Loss and Waste Reduction (Act No. 19 of 2019, promulgated 31 May 2019, in force 1 October).

keyfacts.text: The Muromachi-period dictionary Gagakushu (1444) glosses mottai in its section on words as shotainashi, without proper form, and explains mottainashi as "greatly losing right reason". The Nihon kokugo daijiten gives the first use of mottainashi as A Collection of Tales from Uji (c.1221).

The old-language dictionary gives the senses as (1) outrageous, improper (Tales from Uji 1.15, "ahare, mottainaki aruji kana"), (2) too good for one, gratifying (the kyogen play Buaku, "ah, mottainai, first let me take this hand and help you up"), (3) mottainai, a shame.

The third edition of Kojien (1983) gives three senses, "(1) unseemly towards gods, buddhas or persons of rank; improper. (2) too good for one; undeserved; gratifying. (3) a shame to spend or use up carelessly", and today almost only the third is used.

Wangari Maathai came to Japan in February 2005 at the invitation of the Mainichi Shimbun and met the word mottainai, and on 4 March 2005, in a speech at UN headquarters in New York, proposed "let us spread MOTTAINAI to the world". The same day the Mainichi Shimbun set up a secretariat and began the campaign. She carried it further at Live 8 that July.
The Act on Promotion of Food Loss and Waste Reduction is Act No. 19 of 2019, promulgated on 31 May 2019 and in force from 1 October 2019.
Neither mottainai nor MOTTAINAI is among the words awarded, as grand prize or top ten, in the 22nd New Words and Buzzwords Award of 2005.

011.name: Romantic Love
011.hitokoto: The first use of renai in Japanese is not a book on love but a translation of Self-Help.
body: Renai is not a rewording of the Edo period's iro or koi. The first use cited by the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is the phrase "fell deeply in renai" in Saigoku risshihen (1870-71), Masanao Nakamura's translation of Smiles's Self-Help; the word entered Japan tucked inside a textbook of getting on in the world, not a book that talks about love. As a Chinese compound it was already in Lobscheid's English and Chinese Dictionary (1866-69) as a rendering of to love.

In the first years of Meiji it was used as a rendering of love alongside airen and renbo, and renai came to predominate in the Meiji 20s (1887-96). In 1891 Yoshiharu Iwamoto's Jogaku zasshi answered Soho Tokutomi's argument against renai and defended the word, and in February 1892 Tokoku Kitamura wrote "The Pessimist Poet and Womanhood" in the same magazine and declared that "renai is the secret key to human life". Here the word became a norm.

Honyakugo seiritsu jijo by Akira Yanabu (Iwanami Shinsho, 1982) shows that in letters of 1887 Tokoku wrote "love" in katakana and distinguished it from carnal desire, and argues that because the translated word renai was purified into a Western notion that separates soul from body, its realisation became hard to find within Japanese reality. The word arrived in 1870 and became a commodity in 1892.

made.label: 1870 Saigoku risshihen
made.fact: The first use of renai cited by the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is in Masanao Nakamura's translation Saigoku risshihen (1870-71): "he once saw a girl of the village, fell deeply in renai, and went to her house". Its note on the word says that from the first years of Meiji it was used alongside airen and renbo as a rendering of the English love, and that renai came to predominate from the Meiji 20s (1887-96). It was made a norm by Yoshiharu Iwamoto in Jogaku zasshi in 1890 and by Tokoku Kitamura's "The Pessimist Poet and Womanhood" in the same magazine in February 1892.

keyfacts.text: The first use of renai in the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is in Masanao Nakamura's translation Saigoku risshihen (1870-71): "he once saw a girl of the village, fell deeply in renai, and went to her house".

The same dictionary's note on the word: in China it already appears in Lobscheid's English and Chinese Dictionary (1866-69). In Japan it was used from the first years of Meiji alongside airen and renbo as a rendering of love, and renai came to predominate from the Meiji 20s (1887-96).

The chapter on renai in Honyakugo seiritsu jijo by Akira Yanabu (Iwanami Shinsho, 1982): in letters of 18 August and 4 September 1887, Tokoku Kitamura wrote "love" in katakana and distinguished "the Japanese way of love" from carnal desire. It argues that the translated word renai was purified into a notion separating soul from body, apart from the earlier koi and ai, and that its realisation therefore became hard to find within Japanese reality.

In 1891 Yoshiharu Iwamoto's Jogaku zasshi answered Soho Tokutomi's argument against renai and defended the word, and in February 1892 Tokoku Kitamura published "The Pessimist Poet and Womanhood" in the same magazine, declaring at its opening that "renai is the secret key to human life".

Karyu shunwa (1878-79), Jun'ichiro Oda's translation of Bulwer-Lytton's Ernest Maltravers (1837), depicted love and marriage as an early Meiji translated novel and helped the notion of romantic love take hold.

012.name: Punctuality
012.hitokoto: A foreign instructor in the 1850s wrote that Japanese leisureliness was astounding.
body: On 14 October 1872 (12 September Meiji 5) a railway opened between Shinbashi and Yokohama. The timetable was written in hours and minutes, but what people used was the variable-hour system, which divided day and night each into six, and whose smallest unit, the kohanko, was about 30 minutes. Trains to the minute had begun to run over a reckoning of time whose hours changed length with the season.

Two months later, on 9 November Meiji 5, Grand Council Proclamation No. 337, "The Rescript on the Calendar Change and the Promulgation of the Solar Calendar", was issued; 3 December Meiji 5 became 1 January Meiji 6, and the day switched to fixed hours, 24 to the day. Willem van Kattendijke, the Dutch officer who taught at the Nagasaki Naval Training Centre in the last years of the shogunate, left the words "the leisureliness of the Japanese is astounding". A people that keeps time does not yet exist at this point.

Chikoku no tanjo, edited by Takehiko Hashimoto and Shigehisa Kuriyama (Sangensha, 2001), follows the process by which railways, factories and schools drilled in time discipline, and argues that there was a stretch of the Meiji period when late arrivals on the railways were normal, and that running to time became strict only from about 1900. In 1887 service regulations were made to bring station clocks and conductors' watches into line, and in 1920 the Life Improvement League made 10 June Time Day. Manufacture took half a century.

made.label: 1873 Fixed hours in force
made.fact: On 14 October 1872 (12 September Meiji 5) the railway between Shinbashi and Yokohama opened, with a timetable in hours and minutes. Grand Council Proclamation No. 337 of 9 November Meiji 5, "The Rescript on the Calendar Change and the Promulgation of the Solar Calendar", made 3 December Meiji 5 into 1 January Meiji 6 (1 January 1873), abolished the variable-hour system and switched to fixed hours, 24 to the day.

keyfacts.text: Grand Council Proclamation No. 337 of 9 November Meiji 5, "The Rescript on the Calendar Change and the Promulgation of the Solar Calendar". It made 3 December Meiji 5 into 1 January Meiji 6 and introduced fixed hours, with 365 days to the year and 24 hours to the day.

On 14 October 1872 (12 September Meiji 5) Japan's first railway opened over the 29 km between Shinbashi and Yokohama. From the first day the timetable was in minutes, showing people a finer division of time than the smallest unit of Edo's variable hours, the kohanko of about 30 minutes.
In 1887 the Service Regulations for Staff Employed on Operating Lines were laid down, requiring station clocks and conductors' watches to be brought into line.

Willem van Kattendijke, the Dutch naval officer who taught at the Nagasaki Naval Training Centre in the last years of the shogunate (1857-59), recorded in Nagasaki kaigun denshujo no hibi that "the leisureliness of the Japanese is astounding", giving as examples timber ordered for the tide that did not arrive and workmen who did not come back to the yard.

Chikoku no tanjo: The Formation of Time Consciousness in Modern Japan, edited by Takehiko Hashimoto and Shigehisa Kuriyama (Sangensha, August 2001), follows the formation of time discipline through railways, factories and schools, and argues that there was a stretch of the Meiji period when late arrivals on the railways were normal, and that running to time grew strict only from about 1900.

In 1920, during the "Time" exhibition planned by the Ministry of Education and held at the Tokyo Museum of Education from 16 May to 4 July, the Life Improvement League and other supporting bodies fixed 10 June as Time Day. It derives from the entry in the Nihon shoki on the setting up of a water clock on the 25th day of the fourth month of Tenji 10.

013.name: Maternal Instinct
013.hitokoto: It was a Ministry of Health and Welfare white paper that denied the three-year-old myth.
body: Bosei is held to be a translated word set against the moderskap of the Swedish thinker Ellen Key. By the time Akiko Yosano wrote "Against the Overvaluing of Motherhood" for the February 1916 issue of Taiyo it was current enough to carry a title, and it spread with The Renaissance of Motherhood, translated by Raicho Hiratsuka (Shinchosha, 1919). The first use in the Nihon kokugo daijiten is likewise Takeo Arishima's A Certain Woman of 1919.

In the debate on the protection of motherhood of 1918-19, Yosano, who argued for women's economic independence, was set against Hiratsuka, who held that the state should protect women through pregnancy, birth and child-rearing. The notion that a mother's love is instinct got its word in this period, and in household-education books of the 1910s and 1920s it is stressed as "a heart that gives itself for the child". Before that, as Mikako Sawayama's work shows, child-rearing in early-modern times sat next to borrowed milk and service as a wet nurse, to fostering out, to abandonment and infanticide.

Boseiai shinwa no wana by Masami Ohinata (Nippon Hyoron Sha, 2000) argued that "the maternal" is a myth society produced. A government white paper denies part of it too. The 1998 White Paper on Health and Welfare states plainly that "no rational basis, at least, can be found for the three-year-old myth", and wrote that most of child-rearing can be done by fathers as well. No continuing opinion survey was found, within what this catalogue examined, that tracks approval or disapproval of maternal love itself.

made.label: 1916 The word bosei
made.fact: Bosei is held to be a rendering of the Swedish moderskap of Ellen Key. An early use is Akiko Yosano's "Against the Overvaluing of Motherhood" (Taiyo, February 1916), and it came into circulation with The Renaissance of Motherhood, translated by Raicho Hiratsuka (Shinchosha, 1919). The first use given by the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is Takeo Arishima's A Certain Woman (1919). It was widely argued over in the debate on the protection of motherhood of 1918-19, and the word settled in during the Showa period (Nihon joseishi jiten).

keyfacts.text: Nihon joseishi jiten (Shinjinbutsu Oraisha, 1994) takes bosei as a rendering of Ellen Key's moderskap and says it was first used in The Renaissance of Motherhood, translated by Raicho Hiratsuka (Shinchosha, 1919); but Akiko Yosano's "Against the Overvaluing of Motherhood" (Taiyo, February 1916) already uses bosei in its title, so the word was in circulation by 1916.

The first use of bosei in the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is Takeo Arishima's A Certain Woman (1919), "an unstoppable consciousness of bosei". Britannica International Encyclopaedia describes motherhood as "not something with which women are instinctively equipped, but a cultural and social attribute".

The debate on the protection of motherhood (1918-19): Akiko Yosano held up women's economic independence and criticised state protection of motherhood as "a doctrine of dependence"; Raicho Hiratsuka, following Ellen Key, argued for state protection of women through pregnancy, birth and child-rearing.

The 1998 White Paper on Health and Welfare states plainly that "no rational basis, at least, can be found for the three-year-old myth", and said that most of child-rearing is possible for fathers too, and that excessive closeness between mother and child can have ill effects.

Edo no chichi to kodomo by Mikako Sawayama (Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 2017) treats early-modern borrowed milk and service as a wet nurse and the relation of abandoned children to milk, and Shussan to shintai no kinsei (Keiso Shobo, 1998) treats measures against infanticide such as the Sendai domain's infant-rearing scheme. Both show that milk and child-rearing were not shut up in the mother alone.
Boseiai shinwa no wana by Masami Ohinata (Nippon Hyoron Sha, April 2000) argues that "the maternal" is a myth society produced. The same author's Bosei no kenkyu appeared in 1988.

014.name: Nudity Is Shameful
014.hitokoto: A fine for going out naked. The article took effect in Tokyo on 13 November Meiji 5.
body: On 8 November Meiji 5 (8 December 1872) Tokyo Prefecture issued the Ishiki Kaii Regulations, the misdemeanour code, and put them in force from the 13th. Five general articles, 23 ishiki offences, 25 kaii offences. Article 22 made "whoever goes naked or bares the upper body, or exposes the thighs and legs, making an unseemly spectacle", and Article 12 "whoever runs a mixed bath for a living", subject to a fine, with caning or detention where it could not be paid. The Grand Council proclamation of 19 July 1873 turned them into the Local Ishiki Kaii Regulations, in 90 articles, and spread them over the whole country.

Behind this were foreign eyes. Perry's Narrative of the Expedition (1856) drew the mixed bathing of a public bathhouse in Shimoda with an illustration, and judged the common people of Japan lewd for all their high morals. Miki Kawabata argues that rulers who had taken the Western gaze inside regarded the old customs as backward and forbade them. Bans on mixed bathing were not a Meiji invention, though: they had been issued and broken again and again since the Edo period, in Kansei-era Edo, in Kyoto in 1843, in a Tokyo notification of 1869.

What was new was that the bans on nakedness issued in Yokohama in 1868 and Tokyo in 1871 were gathered into regulations with penalties, and those made into national law. The regulations were absorbed into the police offences of the Penal Code of 1880, in force from 1882, and passed on to the Police Offences Punishment Ordinance of 1908 and the Minor Offences Act of 1948. The sense that nakedness is shameful has run 150 years without a break in the text.

made.label: 1872 Misdemeanour regulations
made.fact: Tokyo Prefecture notification of 8 November 1872 (Meiji 5), in force from the 13th of the same month. Article 22 of the ishiki offences, "whoever goes naked or bares the upper body, or exposes the thighs and legs, making an unseemly spectacle", and Article 12, "whoever runs a mixed bath for a living", were made subject to a fine; where it could not be paid, an ishiki offence drew caning and a kaii offence detention. The Grand Council proclamation of 19 July 1873 rolled them out nationwide as the Local Ishiki Kaii Regulations, in 90 articles.

keyfacts.text: The Tokyo Ishiki Kaii Regulations were made by a Tokyo Prefecture notification of 8 November 1872 (Meiji 5) and came into force on the 13th of the same month (5 general articles, 23 ishiki offences, 25 kaii offences). The Grand Council proclamation of 19 July 1873 turned them into the Local Ishiki Kaii Regulations, in 90 articles (37 ishiki, 48 kaii), which each locality could add to or cut with the permission of the Police Bureau.

Among the ishiki offences were "Article 12, whoever runs a mixed bath for a living" and "Article 22, whoever goes naked or bares the upper body, or exposes the thighs and legs, making an unseemly spectacle". The Yomiuri Shimbun of 22 January 1876 carries a report of a bathhouse in Hakozaki-cho caught with mixed bathing.

Banning mixed bathing was not a Meiji invention. Mixed baths were forbidden in Edo in the Kansei era (about 1791), in Kyoto in June 1843, at the opening of Tsukiji in 1868, in a Tokyo notification of 1869, and again in Kyoto Prefecture Notification No. 160 of 1871.

Perry's Narrative of the Expedition (1856) drew the mixed bathing of a public bathhouse in Shimoda with an illustration, and judged the lower orders of Japan lewd for all their high morals. The illustration was cut from the later printing.

Miki Kawabata, citing Sumio Ohinata (1992), traces how the accounts of Westerners such as Harris, Perry and Suenson made mixed bathing and nakedness a problem, and how the Japanese side took that gaze inside, regarded the old ways as backward and forbade them.

The Ishiki Kaii Regulations were absorbed into Book 4, "Police Offences", of the Penal Code of 1880 (promulgated 17 July 1880, in force 1 January 1882), and passed on to the Police Offences Punishment Ordinance of 1908 and, after the war, to the Minor Offences Act (1948, exposure of the body).

015.name: Chastity
015.hitokoto: The article punishing a married woman's adultery lost its effect on 15 November 1947.
body: Article 353 of the Penal Code promulgated on 17 July 1880 (Grand Council Proclamation No. 36) punished a married woman's adultery, and the man with her, with major imprisonment of not less than six months and not more than two years. A husband's affair was no crime unless the other party was another man's wife. In February 1899 came the Girls' High School Order (Imperial Ordinance No. 31), and in July that year Education Minister Sukenori Kabayama told the conference of regional school inspectors that the aim of girls' education "lies in laying the groundwork for making them wise mothers and good wives". Chastity was held up by the law and the school alike.

The crime of adultery passed into Article 183 of the Penal Code of 1907 and was deleted by Act No. 124 of 26 October 1947. Yet in January of that same 1947 the Director-General of the Social Education Bureau of the Ministry of Education circulated "On the Implementation of Purity Education", set up a purity education committee the next year, and in 1949 drew up the Basic Outline of Purity Education. The change of name to "sex education" comes around 1970: the norm the law let go of was carried on for a quarter-century by the postwar Ministry of Education.

According to the National Fertility Survey of the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research, the share of unmarried women aged 18 to 34 with no experience of sex fell from 65.3% in 1987 to 36.3% in 2005, then turned back up to 49.4% in 2021, with men back to 44.2%. Chastity as a norm is discontinued, but on the ground the share with no experience of sex is rising again for other reasons. How village customs of premarital relations such as yobai, night visiting, disappeared in modern times is described in works such as Keisuke Akamatsu's Yobai no minzokugaku.

made.label: 1899 Girls' High School Order
made.fact: Article 353 of Grand Council Proclamation No. 36 of 17 July 1880, the Penal Code, punished adultery by a married woman and the man with her with major imprisonment of not less than six months and not more than two years (in force 1 January 1882). Imperial Ordinance No. 31 of 7 February 1899, the Girls' High School Order (published in the Official Gazette on 8 February); at the conference of regional school inspectors in July that year Education Minister Sukenori Kabayama said the aim of higher general education for girls "lies in laying the groundwork for making them wise mothers and good wives".

discontinued.label: 1947 Adultery struck out
discontinued.fact: Following equality under the law in Article 14 of the Constitution of Japan (in force 3 May 1947), Act No. 124 of 26 October 1947, the Act Partially Amending the Penal Code, deleted Article 183 of the Penal Code, the crime of adultery.

keyfacts.text: Penal Code of 1880 (Grand Council Proclamation No. 36 of 17 July 1880, in force 1 January 1882), Article 353: adultery by a married woman drew major imprisonment of not less than six months and not more than two years, and so did the man with her. A husband's infidelity was not punished.
It passed into Article 183 of the present Penal Code (Act No. 45 of 24 April 1907, in force 1 October 1908) and was deleted by Act No. 124 of 26 October 1947.

The Girls' High School Order is Imperial Ordinance No. 31, sanctioned on 7 February 1899 (Official Gazette, 8 February). In July 1899 Education Minister Sukenori Kabayama told the conference of regional school inspectors that it "lies in laying the groundwork for making them wise mothers and good wives; therefore it cultivates a graceful and lofty temper and a mild and chaste nature".

Purity education after the war: January 1947, the Social Education Bureau Director-General's circular "On the Implementation of Purity Education"; 1948, the purity education committee; 1949, the Basic Outline of Purity Education; 1955, "How to Conduct Purity Education (a draft)". It is replaced by "sex education" around 1970.

National Fertility Survey (National Institute of Population and Social Security Research): unmarried women aged 18 to 34 with no experience of sex, 65.3% in 1987, 36.3% in 2005, 49.4% in 2021. Unmarried men, 43.1%, 31.9% (2005), 44.2% (2021).

How the modern norm of chastity drove out the village custom of premarital relations, yobai or night visiting, is described in works such as Keisuke Akamatsu's Yobai no minzokugaku (Akashi Shoten, 1994).

016.name: Rising in the World
016.hitokoto: Risshin shusse is already in a kabuki play of 1753. What Meiji made was the content.
body: The four characters of risshin shusse are not a Meiji coinage. The first use in the Nihon kokugo daijiten is the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi of 1753, and in the Edo period it meant an ethic of life, keeping to one's station and living frugally in order to "come out into the world and make oneself". What Meiji manufactured was not the word but the content, which was replaced by upward movement through learning and effort.

In 1872 (2 August Meiji 5) the Education System Order was issued with Grand Council Proclamation No. 214, and its preamble taught that "learning is the capital for making one's way" and called on every citizen to attend school. Saigoku risshihen (Smiles's Self-Help), translated by Masanao Nakamura and published two years earlier, and Yukichi Fukuzawa's An Encouragement of Learning, published that same year, became bestsellers, and Risshin shusse shugi by Yo Takeuchi (NHK Books, 1997) describes how this desire became the romance of modern Japan.

In a century and a half the goods have faded. In the Global Survey on Employment and Growth Awareness by Persol Research and Consulting (2022, 18 countries and regions), 19.8% of rank-and-file employees in Japan said they wanted to become managers, the lowest of all, against 90.5% in India, which came first. In 2021 oya-gacha, the parent lottery, entered the top ten of the New Words and Buzzwords Award. The notion that drove out being decided by birth is being driven back by being decided by birth.

made.label: 1872 The Education System Order
made.fact: Grand Council Proclamation No. 214 of 2 August Meiji 5, the preamble on the encouragement of learning: "Learning may be called the capital for making one's way." Saigoku risshihen (1870-71), translated by Masanao Nakamura, and Yukichi Fukuzawa's An Encouragement of Learning (1872) became bestsellers, and risshin shusse turned into the sense of upward movement through learning. The phrase itself is used in the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi (1753).

keyfacts.text: The first use of risshin shusse in the Nihon kokugo daijiten, selected edition, is the kabuki play Osanago no katakiuchi (1753): "if only you will hand over the certificate, rising in the world is in plain sight". The phrase exists from the middle of the Edo period.

Encyclopedia Nipponica: in the Edo period risshin shusse was an ethic of life, frugal and holding to one's station, of "coming out into the world and making oneself", but after the Meiji Restoration it was tied to upward social movement and later institutionalised through the school and the bureaucracy.

The preamble to the Education System Order, Grand Council Proclamation No. 214 of 2 August Meiji 5, states that "learning may be called the capital for making one's way" and called on every citizen to attend school.

Risshin shusse shugi: Romance and Desire in Modern Japan by Yo Takeuchi was published as NHK Books in November 1997, with an enlarged edition from Sekaishisosha in 2005. It expands the text of the NHK Ningen Daigaku series (January to March 1996), "Risshin shusse and the Japanese".

In the Global Survey on Employment and Growth Awareness by Persol Research and Consulting (surveyed February to March 2022, published November, 18 countries and regions), rank-and-file employees saying they wanted to become managers were 19.8% in Japan, the lowest of all (India first at 90.5%, Vietnam second at 87.8%).
Oya-gacha was chosen for the top ten of the 2021 U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award, and took the grand prize in the Daijisen New Word of the Year 2021.

017.name: Bushido
017.hitokoto: Bushido was written in English; a Japanese reader had to wait eight years.
body: Inazo Nitobe's Bushido: The Soul of Japan came out in English in 1900, from Leeds & Biddle of Philadelphia (the copyright notice reads 1899). The Japanese translation, by Oson Sakurai, came in March 1908; until then it was read in the English reprint issued by Shokabo of Tokyo in 1900. The representative at home of the argument that identified bushido with national morality is Tetsujiro Inoue, who began with Bushido (Heiji Zasshisha) in 1901 and in 1905 edited the three-volume Bushido sosho with Sukemasa Arima.

The word itself, however, is not of 1900 make. Bushido first appears in Koyo gunkan, compiled in the early Edo period, where it was the technique by which an individual samurai made his name and survived. Hagakure (about 1716) was a secret book of the Saga domain and had never been in print until an abridgement edited by Ikuichi Nakamura appeared in 1906, and the Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors of 1882 preached not bushido but chusetsu, fidelity.

Bushido no gyakushu by Kakumyo Kanno (Kodansha Gendai Shinsho, 2004) argued that the "Meiji bushido" made in the years of the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese wars is a different thing from the bushido of before modern times, and Oleg Benesch called the same process an invention in Inventing the Way of the Samurai (2014). The word is 17th-century stock; the meaning is a new product of the late Meiji period. It has been discussed as a textbook case of what Hobsbawm called an invented tradition.

made.label: 1900 Nitobe's Bushido
made.fact: Inazo Nitobe's Bushido: The Soul of Japan was published in 1900 by Leeds & Biddle of Philadelphia (copyright notice 1899). At home, writing on bushido was turned out in quantity from Tetsujiro Inoue's Bushido (Heiji Zasshisha, 1901) onward, and the three-volume Bushido sosho was edited in 1905. Nitobe's Japanese translation is that of Oson Sakurai (Teibi Shuppansha, March 1908). The word first appears in Koyo gunkan, compiled in the early Edo period.

keyfacts.text: The oldest edition held by the National Diet Library is Bushido; the soul of Japan, Philadelphia: Leeds & Biddle, 1900 (copyright 1899). It carries no statement that it is a first edition, and Nakajima, "On the confusion over the bibliographical details of Inazo Nitobe's Bushido" (2008), points out the confusion in the bibliography.
The first Japanese translation is Bushido, translated by Oson Sakurai (Teibi Shuppansha, March 1908).
The first book to write down the word bushido is Koyo gunkan, compiled in the early Edo period, where it was conceived as the technique by which an individual samurai made his name and survived.

Hagakure was a secret book of the Saga domain, and its first appearance in print was an abridgement, about a fifth of the original, edited by Ikuichi Nakamura and published in Tokyo on 23 March 1906. In February 1911 it was reissued, borrowing the fame of Maresuke Nogi, as Nabeshima rongo Hagakure.

The Imperial Rescript to Soldiers and Sailors of 1882 preached not bushido but chusetsu, fidelity. A "bushido boom" followed the Sino-Japanese War (1894-95), and from Bushido (Heiji Zasshisha) in 1901 onward Tetsujiro Inoue developed the argument identifying bushido with national morality, editing Bushido sosho in three volumes (30 March, 18 June and 25 November 1905).

Bushido no gyakushu by Kakumyo Kanno (Kodansha Gendai Shinsho, 20 October 2004) treats the bushido of the boom as an image made from Meiji onward, and argues in chapter 5, "Meiji bushido", for its break with early-modern times. Oleg Benesch, Inventing the Way of the Samurai (Oxford UP, 2014) and Yasushi Suzuki, "The creation of bushido in Meiji Japan", likewise treat Meiji bushido as a creation or invention.

018.name: Diligence as Virtue
018.hitokoto: Japanese diligence, Yasumaru argued, is a morality spread in the late Edo period.
body: Nihon no kindaika to minshu shiso (Japan's Modernisation and Popular Thought) by Yoshio Yasumaru (Aoki Shoten, 1974) argued that a "conventional morality" of diligence, thrift, filial piety and honesty spread from the late early-modern period through the years of the Restoration as a discipline the people laid on themselves, and became the spiritual base of modernisation. Its textbooks were the Shingaku of Baigan Ishida and the hotoku method of Sontoku Ninomiya, and Yasumaru drew this not as a virtue of the samurai but as a discipline farmers and townsmen imposed on themselves.

In a paper to the Socio-Economic History Society in 1976, "The formation of economic society and its characteristics" (published 1977), Akira Hayami named the agriculture of the Edo period, which raised output by cutting livestock and adding human labour, an "industrious revolution". It carries the year made back to the 17th and 18th centuries, earlier than Yasumaru. On either account diligence is not an ancient national character but something that spread at a particular time in the Edo period.

The figures point downhill. In the Monthly Labour Survey, annual total hours actually worked per regular employee went from 2,432 in 1960 to 2,052 in 1990 and 1,693 in 2025. Much of that is the move to a 40-hour week under the 1987 amendment to the Labour Standards Act, and the rising share of part-time workers, whose hours are short; it is not a figure that shows a change in the sense of diligence directly.

made.label: Late Edo Conventional morality
made.fact: Nihon no kindaika to minshu shiso by Yoshio Yasumaru (Aoki Shoten, September 1974) argued that a "conventional morality" of diligence, thrift, filial piety and honesty spread from the late early-modern period to the years of the Restoration as the self-discipline of the people, and became the spiritual base of modernisation. The Shingaku of Baigan Ishida (1685-1744) and the hotoku method of Sontoku Ninomiya (1787-1856) are the representative cases. In a paper to the 1976 meeting of the Socio-Economic History Society, "The formation of economic society and its characteristics" (published 1977), Akira Hayami proposed an "industrious revolution" in the Edo period, carrying the year made further back.

keyfacts.text: Nihon no kindaika to minshu shiso by Yoshio Yasumaru was published by Aoki Shoten on 1 September 1974 (reissued in the Heibonsha Library in 1999). It set out the process by which a "conventional morality" of diligence, thrift and self-denial took root in the minds of ordinary people and became the spiritual base of modernisation.

The term "industrious revolution" was first used explicitly by Akira Hayami in his paper "The formation of economic society and its characteristics", given at the 1976 meeting of the Socio-Economic History Society (common theme: "In search of a new picture of the Edo period") and published in 1977.

In the Monthly Labour Survey (establishments with 30 or more employees), annual total hours actually worked per regular employee averaged 2,432 in 1960, 2,239 in 1970, 2,052 in 1990, 1,859 in 2000, 1,685 in 2020 and 1,693 in 2025 (the series before 1969 excludes services). For establishments with 5 or more employees it is 1,621 in 2025.

Behind the fall in hours lie changes of rule such as the 1987 amendment to the Labour Standards Act, which cut statutory hours in stages from 48 to 40 a week, and from the late 1990s the rising share of part-time workers also tells; it is not an indicator of a change of attitude in itself.

The continuing question closest to "work is a virtue" is in the NHK Broadcasting Culture Research Institute's "Japanese Value Orientations" survey (every five years from 1973, the work-oriented and leisure-oriented answers under "work and leisure").

019.name: Family at the Table
019.hitokoto: The chabudai spread across Japan by early Showa and gave way to tables by 1980.
body: Calling the place where life is lived katei rose sharply, above all in the magazines, in the years from 1887, and was taken as the translation of the English home. In the Nihon kokugo daijiten the first attested use in the sense of the place where husband and wife, parents and children live is Koyo Ozaki's Konjiki yasha (1897-98) — the word katei itself has a use in Shinbun zasshi in 1871 — and until then kanai and ie were the main words. Soho Tokutomi's Min'yusha launched Katei zasshi in September 1892, and Senryaku toshite no kazoku (The Family as Strategy) by Kazue Muta (Shin'yosha, 1996) argues that the ideology of katei appeared around 1887.

The word came first, however, and the table after. The chabudai, the single low table a family sits round, appeared about 1887, and spread across the country from the end of Taisho into the early Showa years; before that each person had a hakozen, an individual tray (Chabudai no Showa, edited by Kazuko Koizumi, Kawade Shobo Shinsha). With individual trays the father took the head place and the mother the lower one, and "it was not an atmosphere for talking during a meal", while after the change to the chabudai "it became easier to talk", one witness recalls (interviews in Seika, Kyoto).

The word danran itself has a use, "the whole house in a circle", in Sodoshu, a collection of Chinese poems of 1816, so it is not of Meiji make. What Meiji made was the idea that katei is home, and what spread from the end of Meiji into the early Showa years was the shape of the table that reproduced it every evening. The chabudai was replaced by the chair-height table from the late 1950s, and the changeover was complete in the 1980s. The traditional scene of the family in a circle was on sale for about 60 years.
