037.name: Kizuna
037.hitokoto: In the Diet of 1950, kizuna was something to escape. By 2011, something to deepen.
body: The second sense of kizuna in the dictionaries is still "a rope for tethering a horse or other animal". Its old reading was hodashi, that is, a fetter. Gather the statements containing the character in the record of Diet proceedings just after the war and most are uses meaning restraint, such as "to escape the fetters of the government" and "the fetters of the Empire", along with makikyahan, the puttee. Even around 1980 the main use was "the binding force of law", and the approving "firm bonds" was in the minority.

The collocations "the bonds of family" and "the bonds of community" enter the vocabulary of politics only from the end of the 1990s. The first appearance of "the bonds of family" in the record of Diet proceedings is 2 June 1998, as a quotation from the basic policy of the Liberal Party. In May 2006 the government made a project team of parliamentary secretaries under the banner of "restoring the bonds of family and community". "The bonds of community" becomes frequent in the Diet only after the prime minister's policy speech of 2009. In 1995, the year of the Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake, the word was spoken only five times.

On 12 December 2011 the Kanji of the Year announced at Kiyomizu-dera was kizuna. Sixty-one thousand votes out of about 497,000. The New Words and Buzzwords Award for the year also put it in the top ten, but named no recipient. Stock that had been a tethering rope was reshipped, in an emergency, as the word for connection in the year of the disaster.

made.label: 1998 The bonds of family
made.fact: The first appearance of "the bonds of family" in the record of Diet proceedings is 2 June 1998, in the House of Councillors Special Committee on Administrative and Fiscal Reform and the Tax System (Yuzuru Tsuzuki quoting the Liberal Party's basic policy, "a people that values the bonds of family and loves its country"). For "the bonds of community", the government set up in May 2006 a project team of the parliamentary secretaries' meeting on restoring the bonds of family and community (it becomes frequent in the Diet only after Prime Minister Hatoyama's policy speech of October 2009) (17 March 2009, House of Councillors Committee on Cabinet, Eriko Yamatani).

restocked.label: 2011 Kanji of the Year
restocked.fact: On 12 December 2011 the Japan Kanji Aptitude Testing Foundation announced at Kiyomizu-dera that the Kanji of the Year was kizuna. It took 61,453 of 496,997 votes (12.36%), ahead of sai (disaster) with 28,648 and shin (quake) with 26,972. Kizuna also made the top ten of the New Words and Buzzwords Award that year (with no recipient).

keyfacts.text: The Kanji of the Year for 2011 was kizuna. Seihan Mori, chief priest of Kiyomizu-dera, wrote it out on 12 December. Of 496,997 votes in all (the most up to then), kizuna took 61,453, ahead of sai (disaster) 28,648, shin (quake) 26,972, ha (wave) 17,832 and jo (help) 14,011.

The grand prize of the New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2011 went to "Nadeshiko Japan". Kizuna made the top ten but had no recipient. The official note: "The Great East Japan Earthquake, a disaster without precedent, made people recognise afresh the importance of 'kizuna'." Kizuna is also among the 60 nominations (No. 14).

The definition in Digital Daijisen: "(1) A connection between people that cannot be severed; a bond hard to part from. 'The bonds of husband and wife.' (2) A rope for tethering a horse or other animal." It has the verb reading hodasu, and hodashi is an older form of the word for the same rope.

Of the 56 statements containing the character in the record of Diet proceedings for 1947-51, most carry the sense of restraint, such as "to escape the fetters" and "to get away from the fetters of the government", or are makikyahan, the puttee. Even for 1972-81 the main uses are "the binding force of law" and "the fetters of the Empire", and the approving "firm bonds" is in the minority.

Statements containing the character in the record of Diet proceedings stood at only five in 1995, the year of the Great Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake; there were 37 in 2011 and 14 in 2012. "The bonds of family" appears only from 1998, and "the bonds of community" only from 2006.

On 27 January 2011, before the disaster, Azuma Koshiishi said in a plenary session of the House of Councillors that "the bonds of family, of parent and child, of brothers, of husband and wife; the bonds of local society, of the neighbourhood, the school, the workplace … many bonds in present-day society are at times loosening, at times fraying": kizuna was in the vocabulary of politics before the disaster.

curve.title: Statements in the record of Diet proceedings containing ◆the character kizuna
curve.subtitle: to 2024
curve.note: The number of statements containing the character, counted year by year in the Diet Proceedings Search System. Because the record of the most recent years is slow to be included, the chart goes up to 2024. Statements containing kihan (fetters), kyahan (gaiters) and bansoko (sticking plaster), and misprints in the record such as shin-ban-sen for shinkansen, are included in the count.

038.name: Time Performance
038.hitokoto: Taipa took a dictionary publisher's new-word prize in 2022, the Diet in February 2023.
body: Taipa was in use by 2016, but the date on which it was picked as a new word is known. On 30 November 2022 it took the grand prize in "New Words of the Year 2022", chosen by the dictionary editors at Sanseido. Short for "time performance", it measures satisfaction against the time spent. The selection page explains that it is a play on cost performance, kosupa. It was not even nominated for the New Words and Buzzwords Award that year: only the dictionary side picked it up.

The ground had been prepared the year before. In a March 2021 survey by Cross Marketing of 1,100 people aged 20 to 69, about three in ten had watched video at double speed, and among men in their twenties 54.5%. In April 2022 Toyoshi Inada titled the third chapter of his People Who Watch Films on Fast-Forward (Kobunsha Shinsho) "The curse of individuality and the supremacy of 'taipa'".

In the record of Diet proceedings the word was first spoken on 22 February 2023, by a witness who was a researcher at a think tank; a member used it in April that year, and on 13 May 2025 a Parliamentary Vice-Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries answered that "with what is called taipa being valued". It looks the youngest on the shelf, but as a criterion of judgement that grudges time it can also be placed in the line of descent from punctuality.

made.label: 2022 New Word of the Year
made.fact: On 30 November 2022, taipa was chosen as the grand prize of Sanseido's "New Words of the Year 2022", picked by the people who make dictionaries (1,041 entries in all, 673 different words). It is short for "time performance", the effect or satisfaction gained against the time spent.

keyfacts.text: Sanseido's "New Words of the Year 2022" (announced 30 November 2022): grand prize taipa, second "the X construction", third kimazu. Taipa was also among the candidates put up by Hiroaki Iima for the Sanseido Kokugo Jiten and by the Daijirin editorial department.
Taipa is not among the 30 nominations for the 39th New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2022. The grand prize went to "Murakami-sama".

Toyoshi Inada, People Who Watch Films on Fast-Forward: Fast Movies, Spoilers - The Present Form of Content Consumption (Kobunsha Shinsho) went on sale in bookshops on 11 April 2022 (colophon 30 April), 304 pages. The third chapter is titled "People Who Do Not Want to Fail: The Curse of Individuality and the Supremacy of 'Taipa'".

In Cross Marketing's "Survey on Watching Video at Double Speed (2021)" (conducted 5 March 2021, 1,100 men and women aged 20 to 69, published 10 March), about three in ten overall had "experience" of watching at double speed, and 54.5% of men in their twenties.

The first appearance of taipa in the record of Diet proceedings is 22 February 2023, in the House of Councillors Research Committee on National Life, the Economy and the Regions, by a witness, Naoko Kuga of the NLI Research Institute. The first member to use it was Mamoru Umetani, House of Representatives Committee on Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, 12 April 2023. On the government side, Parliamentary Vice-Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries Kenichi Shoji answered "with what is called taipa being valued" in the House of Representatives Committee on Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries on 13 May 2025.

Wikipedia has it that "time performance" was coined by Yohei Harada in 2015, but Harada used "time performance" at the announcement of the "an" white paper on young people in February 2016, and an example of taipa appears in an IT company's column of October that year.

039.name: Oshi-Katsu
039.hitokoto: In 2021, as Idol, Burning took the Akutagawa Prize, oshi-katsu missed the top ten.
body: Oshi-katsu has never been picked for the buzzwords award. In November 2021 it was among the 30 nominations for the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award (No. 07), but did not stay in the top ten. On 20 January of the same year, Rin Usami's Idol, Burning took the 164th Akutagawa Prize. The novel had been published by Kawade Shobo Shinsha on 11 September the year before, and its author was 21.

The word's prehistory runs a little longer. The nominations for the same award in 2011 included oshi-men (No. 09). Wikipedia goes further back, giving as its origin the song-prize races of the 1980s and a feature on Onyanko Club, but that has not been checked against a primary source. In Sanseido's "New Words of the Year", the editorial departments of Daijirin and Shin Meikai Kokugo Jiten have put oshi-katsu up as a candidate every year from 2022 to 2025. Digital Daijisen, meanwhile, already has an entry for it.

Oshi-katsu first appears in the record of Diet proceedings on 29 February 2024, at a public hearing of the House of Representatives Budget Committee, where a professor at Nihon University called political fundraising party tickets "oshi-katsu, to put it in today's way of speaking". In 2025 there were six statements. It is young to be shelved as a view of life, but the record shows it rising.

made.label: 2021 A buzzword nominee
made.fact: Oshi-men was nominated for the New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2011 (No. 09). Rin Usami's Idol, Burning was published on 11 September 2020 and took the 164th Akutagawa Prize on 20 January 2021. Oshi-katsu was nominated for the award for 2021 (No. 07, outside the top ten).

keyfacts.text: Oshi-men is among the 60 nominations for the New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2011 (No. 09), and oshi-katsu among the 30 nominations for 2021 (No. 07). Neither made the top ten. The grand prize for 2021 went to "real nitoryu / Sho-Time".

Rin Usami's Idol, Burning was published by Kawade Shobo Shinsha on 11 September 2020 (ISBN 978-4-309-02916-0). On 20 January 2021 it was awarded the 164th Akutagawa Prize (for the second half of 2020). The author was 21, the third-youngest ever after Risa Wataya and Hitomi Kanehara.

In Sanseido's "New Words of the Year", the Daijirin editorial department put oshi-katsu up as a candidate in 2022, the Shin Meikai Kokugo Jiten department in 2023, and both departments in 2024 and 2025.

The first appearance of oshi-katsu in the record of Diet proceedings is the public hearing of the House of Representatives Budget Committee on 29 February 2024, Kaori Suetomi, professor at Nihon University: "I think it is oshi-katsu, to put it in today's way of speaking" (in the context of political fundraising party tickets). On 14 June 2024 Koji Nakakita, professor at Chuo University, spoke of "oshi-katsu for parties and politicians". There were six statements in 2025.

On the origin of oshi, Wikipedia gives the use by record companies in the song-prize races of the 1980s, pushing a newcomer as their oshi, and a feature on Yuyake Nyan Nyan in which Masanori Ito asked "who is your oshi among the Onyanko?" (on secondary sources).

040.name: Konkatsu
040.hitokoto: Konkatsu was coined in AERA in 2007. It lost the buzzwords award two years running.
body: Konkatsu was born in the AERA of 5 November 2007. Its first appearance is an article in which the family sociologist Masahiro Yamada, on the model of shukatsu, short for job-hunting activity, argued that marriage too is not something that comes to those who wait but something to be got by activity. In February the next year, 2008, The Age of "Konkatsu", written with Toko Shirakawa, was published, and the word spread at once.

In Jiyu Kokuminsha's New Words and Buzzwords Award it was among the nominations two years running, in 2008 and 2009, but reached the top ten in neither. The word settled in all the same, and in 2010 The Sociology of the "Konkatsu" Phenomenon appeared under Yamada's editorship, making it a subject of academic examination.

The state moved too. The supplementary budget for fiscal 2013 created the Grant for Strengthening Regional Measures against the Declining Birth Rate, and marriage-support projects run by local authorities came to be backed with national money. A word put on the market as a personal view of life turned, within a few years, into the name of an administrative measure.

made.label: 2007 Named in AERA
made.fact: The word appeared in AERA of 5 November 2007 (vol. 20, no. 49, whole number 1077), in the article "Preparation: If You Want to Marry, Try 'Konkatsu'" (Toko Shirakawa and Keiko Kimura), as a word coined by the family sociologist Masahiro Yamada on the model of shukatsu, the job hunt.

keyfacts.text: The first appearance of konkatsu is the article "Preparation: If You Want to Marry, Try 'Konkatsu'" (Toko Shirakawa and Keiko Kimura) in AERA of 5 November 2007. Imidas records that "konkatsu first appears in November 2007, from Masahiro Yamada (family sociologist) in the magazine AERA".
Masahiro Yamada and Toko Shirakawa, The Age of "Konkatsu" (Discover Keisho 21, Discover 21), went on sale on 29 February 2008 (the National Diet Library record gives March 2008).

In the New Words and Buzzwords Award it was among the 60 nominations for 2008 (the 25th) but outside the top ten, and was nominated again in 2009 (the 26th), again without making the top ten. The grand prizes for 2008 were "arafo" and "Gu~!".
Masahiro Yamada, ed., The Sociology of the "Konkatsu" Phenomenon: Spouse Selection in Japan Today (Toyo Keizai) was published in June 2010, making it a subject of academic examination.

The Grant for Strengthening Regional Measures against the Declining Birth Rate, which backs local authorities' marriage support financially, was created in the supplementary budget for fiscal 2013 (Heisei 25) and aimed at "seamless support" for marriage, pregnancy, childbirth and child-rearing (later the Grant for the Priority Promotion of Regional Measures against the Declining Birth Rate).

041.name: Shukatsu
041.hitokoto: Preparing for death got a name on 14 August 2009; three years later, a buzzword.
body: Shukatsu is a word born in "Gendai shukatsu jijo", a series that began in the issue of Shukan Asahi dated 14 August 2009. Naming the preparation of a funeral and a grave after shukatsu, job hunting, is credited to Hiroto Sasaki, then deputy editor of the magazine. The series ran to the issue of 25 December that year, following changes in funerals, graves and temples.

The next year, 2010, it was among the nominated words of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award, and in 2012 it was chosen for the top ten. The recipient was Tetsuo Kaneko, a distribution journalist who had prepared his own wake and funeral while alive and died suddenly at 41 in October that year; the editor of Shukan Asahi took the stage at the ceremony, and a letter from his widow was read out in his place.

In a survey the Cabinet Office ran in October 2024 among people aged 60 and over, 60.0% had prepared at least one of seven items: a funeral, a grave, the sorting of property or of possessions, an ending note and the rest. A word that had been the title of a magazine series became, in fifteen years, a frame for analysing what most older people do.

made.label: 2009 Shukan Asahi
made.fact: The word first appears in "Gendai shukatsu jijo", a series that ran in Shukan Asahi from the issue of 14 August 2009 (vol. 114 no. 37, whole no. 4960) to that of 25 December the same year (whole no. 4985). The coinage is credited to Hiroto Sasaki, then deputy editor of the magazine.

keyfacts.text: The first instalment is in Shukan Asahi of 14 August 2009, "Gendai shukatsu jijo: all's well that ends well, the changing shape of funerals"; the last is in the issue of 25 December 2009, "Gendai shukatsu jijo (final instalment): a frank round-table on funerals and graves".
The coinage is credited to Hiroto Sasaki, then deputy editor of Shukan Asahi (he himself works as "the father of shukatsu").

In the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award it was a nominated word in 2010 (the 27th) and reached the top ten in 2012 (the 29th). The recipient for 2012 was Tetsuo Kaneko, a distribution journalist who died suddenly at 41 in October that year (the official form of the name is "the late Mr Tetsuo Kaneko (Shukan Asahi editorial department / distribution journalist)").

In the Cabinet Office Survey on the Economic Life of Older People for fiscal 2024 (conducted October 2024, aged 60 and over, n=2049), 60.0% had prepared at least one of seven items — a funeral, a grave, the sorting of property, the sorting of possessions, an ending note, a living will and so on — that is, were "doing shukatsu"; 40.0% had not.

Rates by item in the same survey: sorting one's own possessions 29.8%, preparing a funeral 21.8%, preparing a grave 21.8%, sorting property 13.6%, writing an ending note 8.3%, writing a living will 3.5%.

042.name: Parent Gacha
042.hitokoto: 150 years after the edicts on surnames and swords, oya-gacha made the 2021 top ten.
body: Oya-gacha comes from the gacha, the paid random draw of smartphone games. The self-mocking line that which parents you are born to is a draw you cannot take again was in use online from about 2015, and when the sociologist Takayoshi Doi wrote about it in Gendai Business on 7 September 2021 it came out all at once as a word for inequality.

On 1 December that year, Jiyu Kokuminsha's U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award chose it for the top ten, and Shogakukan's Daijisen made it the grand prize of its New Word of the Year. Behind it lies what Ryoji Matsuoka's Kyoiku kakusa, educational inequality (2019), demonstrated: the family and the region a person comes from produce a statistical difference in the level of education finally reached.

A hundred and fifty years after the early-modern status order was taken apart in the Meiji period, the criterion that birth decides has gone as an institution. Oya-gacha is that criterion restocked in the vocabulary of probability, and as self-mockery that protects the speaker. Doi argues it is "not a word for blaming parents but a word with which a child protects itself".

made.label: 2021 Buzzword top ten
made.fact: It was in use online from about 2015 as self-mocking slang modelled on the gacha of smartphone games, and became a matter of dispute with Takayoshi Doi's "The essential reason the word oya-gacha struck young people today so hard" (Gendai Business), published on 7 September 2021. Top ten of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award announced on 1 December that year; grand prize of the Daijisen New Word of the Year 2021.

keyfacts.text: The game usage is seen online from about 2013, and use in the present sense increased in 2015-16. At first it was used as a self-mocking joke.

On 7 September 2021 an essay by Takayoshi Doi (University of Tsukuba) was published in Gendai Business and set off dispute on social media. From then it turned into a serious word for toxic parents and economic inequality.
Top ten of the 2021 (38th) U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award (no recipient). The grand prize for the year was "riaru nitoryu / Sho-Time", the real two-way player.
Grand prize of the Shogakukan Daijisen New Word of the Year 2021 (runner-up jinryu, the flow of people), announced on 1 December 2021.

Ryoji Matsuoka's Kyoiku kakusa: kaiso, chiiki, gakureki, educational inequality by class, region and schooling (Chikuma Shinsho 1422), was published on 4 July 2019 and came third in the Shinsho Grand Prize 2020. It demonstrated that "the level of education a child finally reaches differs with the initial conditions of family and region, about which the child can do nothing".

The Yomiuri Shimbun analysed 18,232 tweets containing oya-gacha between 12 February and 4 April 2022 and reported that the most frequent co-occurring word was "failure". Takayoshi Doi called it "not a word for blaming parents but a word with which a child protects itself".

043.name: Live by What You Love
043.reading: suki na koto de, ikite iku
043.hitokoto: "Live by what you love" is not a proverb. It is advertising copy from 2014.
body: "Live by what you love" circulates like a maxim for living, but it comes from a YouTube brand commercial Google released on 3 October 2014 (Japan time). Set against footage of HIKAKIN and others, the copy was repeated in television and station advertising and spread to the public along with the job title YouTuber.

The effect showed in what children pictured for themselves. In the Japan Association for Financial Planners' tally of essays, "YouTuber" rose in 2017 from 14th to 6th among boys, and in Gakken's White Paper on Elementary School Children, "YouTuber", which first appeared in the free-answer column in 2016, came first among boys in 2019. It was the first time since the survey began in 1989.

What marks this entry is that the "manufacturer" of the view of life is an advertising agency. Living by what you love, in the 2010s, was born in the advertising of a video platform and left a trace in the statistics of career choice within a few years.

made.label: 2014 A YouTube advertisement
made.fact: On 2 October 2014 the official YouTube Japan channel posted "Suki na koto de, ikite iku - HIKAKIN - YouTube TVCM" and the same in a long version, and from that month it ran on television and in transport advertising as Google's YouTube brand commercial.

keyfacts.text: The campaign videos, among them "Suki na koto de, ikite iku - HIKAKIN - YouTube [Long ver.]", carry an upload date on YouTube of 2 October 2014.

ITmedia describes it as "a YouTube campaign video released in October 2014", and 4Gamer writes that "in October 2014, bearing the catchphrase Suki na koto de, ikite iku, it came with television commercials and…".

In the Japan Association for Financial Planners' ranking of "the job elementary school pupils want in future" for 2017 (published 24 April 2018, from a tally of 3,974 essays), "YouTuber" rose among boys from 14th to 6th.

In the August 2019 survey for the Gakken Educational Research Institute's White Paper on Elementary School Children, "YouTuber and other internet broadcasters" came first in the boys' ranking for the first time since the survey began in 1989. "YouTuber" first appeared in the free-answer column of the 2016 survey and rose for three years running. Overall, first was pastry chef, second YouTuber, third doctor.

044.name: FIRE
044.hitokoto: Inkyo has been restocked, now as an English acronym, from a US book of 1992.
body: FIRE is an acronym for Financial Independence, Retire Early: building a state in which the income from one's assets alone covers living costs, and stopping work without waiting for the retirement age. Its origin is Your Money or Your Life, published in the United States in 1992, and the blog Mr. Money Mustache, begun in 2011, spread it as a movement in the 2010s.

It came into Japan as a product in 2020. March brought the translation of Quit Like a Millionaire, by Canadians who had done it, and July Honki de FIRE o mezasu hito no tame no shisan keisei nyumon, an introduction to building assets for those serious about FIRE, by Yuiki Hotaka, a former company employee; in 2021 it was reported as "a movement centred on the young". The Japanese translation of the 1992 book at the origin came after that, in May 2021.

Early-modern inkyo, handing on the headship and stepping back from the front line, and FIRE, getting off work on investment income, do not look alike. But in the sense that a view of life — retiring while still in one's prime — broke off and came back under another name, FIRE can be called restocked inkyo.

made.label: c.2020 Spread in Japan
made.fact: In the United States Vicki Robin and Joe Dominguez's Your Money or Your Life (1992) is the origin of the idea, and the blog Mr. Money Mustache (Peter Adeney), begun in 2011, spread it as a movement in the 2010s. In Japan the translation Quit Like a Millionaire (Diamond, Inc.) appeared in March 2020 and Yuiki Hotaka's Honki de FIRE o mezasu hito no tame no shisan keisei nyumon (Jitsumu Kyoiku Shuppan) in July the same year, and in 2021 it was reported as "a movement centred on the young".

keyfacts.text: Vicki Robin and Joe Dominguez's Your Money or Your Life (1992) set out "the basic template of a simple life achieving financial independence on investment income". Jacob Lund Fisker's Early Retirement Extreme (2010) formalised the relation between the savings rate and the years to retirement.
The blog Mr. Money Mustache (Peter Adeney) began in 2011 and helped spread the FIRE movement. In a Harris Poll of 2018, 11% of well-off Americans aged 45 and over knew FIRE by name.

The Japanese FIRE books are Kristy Shen and Bryce Leung's Quit Like a Millionaire (translated by Masaaki Iwamoto, Diamond, Inc.) in March 2020, and Yuiki Hotaka's Honki de FIRE o mezasu hito no tame no shisan keisei nyumon (Jitsumu Kyoiku Shuppan) on 2 July 2020.
The Japanese translation of Your Money or Your Life, the book at the origin, appeared as Okane ka jinsei ka (Diamond, Inc.) in May 2021, 29 years after the original.
In February 2021 it was reported that "FIRE, becoming financially independent and retiring early, has become a movement centred on the young".
"FIRE" is not among the official nominated words of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2019 to 2023.

045.name: Sustainable
045.hitokoto: Awareness of the SDGs went from 14.8% in 2018 to 86.0% four years later.
body: The current stock of the norm of sustainability is shipped from the SDGs, the Sustainable Development Goals, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 25 September 2015. It is an international agreement to reach 17 goals and 169 targets by 2030, and work began in each country from the following year, 2016.

Its spread among people in Japan can be seen as a line in Dentsu's repeated Consumer Survey on Sustainable Development Goals. Awareness of the word SDGs was 14.8% in February 2018 and flat at 16.0% in 2019, then reached 29.1% in 2020, 54.2% in 2021, 86.0% in 2022 and 91.6% in 2023. Those who "know it down to the content" also rose from 3.6% to 40.4%.

In Jiyu Kokuminsha's U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award, "SDGs" was nominated in 2021, but there is no record of "sustainable" itself. Independently of any award, the line of awareness stood up vertically. It is a case of a word going from the low tens to the eighties of per cent in four years.

made.label: 2015 The SDGs adopted
made.fact: On 25 September 2015 the UN General Assembly adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (the SDGs, 17 goals and 169 targets). In Dentsu's Consumer Survey on Sustainable Development Goals, awareness of the SDGs went 14.8% in February 2018 → 16.0% in February 2019 → 29.1% in January 2020 → 54.2% in January 2021 → 86.0% in January 2022 → 91.6% in February 2023, rising sharply between 2019 and 2021.

keyfacts.text: The SDGs were adopted on 25 September 2015 at the UN Sustainable Development Summit (the General Assembly) as the core of "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development".

Dentsu, third survey (18-19 January 2020): awareness of the SDGs 29.1%, up 13.1 points from "the second survey conducted in February 2019" (second survey 16.0%); "the awareness in the first survey of 2018 (14.8%)".
Dentsu, fourth survey (22-25 January 2021): awareness 54.2% (close to double the 29.1% of the third), "know it down to the content" 20.5%.
Dentsu, fifth survey (17-21 January 2022): awareness 86.0%, "understand it down to the content" 34.2%. Among teenagers, 52.5%.
Dentsu, sixth survey (7-10 February 2023, n=1,400): awareness 91.6%, "know it down to the content" 40.4% (more than eleven times the 3.6% of the first).
In the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award, "SDGs" was a nominated word in 2021 (the 38th), outside the top ten. No award or nomination for "sustainable" on its own exists between 2005 and 2024.

curve.title: Awareness of the word "SDGs"
curve.subtitle: "Know it down to the content" + ◆"do not know the content but have heard the name"

046.name: Danshari
046.hitokoto: Danshari became a book title in December 2009, a buzzword nominee the next year.
body: The view of life that one lives with fewer things became a book under the name danshari in December 2009. Hideko Yamashita's Shin katazuke-jutsu "danshari", a new art of tidying, came out from Magazine House and sold, and the next year, 2010, it was among the nominated words of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award. The word comes from the yoga practices of dangyo, shagyo and rigyo, refusing, discarding and detaching, and Yamashita holds it as a registered trademark.

Marie Kondo's Jinsei ga tokimeku katazuke no maho, published in January 2011, then went out into the world. The English edition, The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up, appeared in October 2014, and in 2015 she was chosen for TIME's 100 most influential people in the world. It is a case of a method of tidying becoming an export out of Japan.

In June 2015 Fumio Sasaki's Boku-tachi ni, mo mono wa hitsuyo nai., we do not need things any more, appeared, and "minimalist" was nominated for the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award that year. Facing the postwar view of life that piled up a house of one's own and durable goods, a shelf of not owning was built up over six years.

made.label: 2009 Danshari published
made.fact: Hideko Yamashita's Shin katazuke-jutsu "danshari" (Magazine House, December 2009) sold well and was nominated for the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award for 2010. Fumio Sasaki's Boku-tachi ni, mo mono wa hitsuyo nai. (Wani Books, June 2015) led to "minimalist" being nominated in 2015.

keyfacts.text: Hideko Yamashita's Shin katazuke-jutsu "danshari": tidying changes your life (Magazine House) was published in December 2009. The word derives from Masahiro Oki's yoga thought of dangyo, shagyo and rigyo, refusing, discarding and detaching, and Yamashita holds it as a registered trademark.
"Danshari" was a nominated word (one of 60) of the 2010 (27th) U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award. It did not reach the top ten.

Marie Kondo's Jinsei ga tokimeku katazuke no maho (Sunmark) is dated January 2011 in the NDL record. The English edition, The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up, appeared in October 2014 (Ten Speed Press), and in 2015 she was chosen for TIME's 100 most influential people in the world.
Fumio Sasaki's Boku-tachi ni, mo mono wa hitsuyo nai. (Wani Books) was published in June 2015. It has been translated into many languages, including the English Goodbye, Things (Penguin, 2017).
"Minimalist" was a nominated word of the 2015 (32nd) U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award. Outside the top ten.

047.name: Reskilling
047.hitokoto: "Investment in people", reskilling included: 1 trillion yen over five years, 2022.
body: Reskilling means workers learning the skills of a new job afresh as technology changes. The World Economic Forum raised the "Reskilling Revolution" at Davos in January 2020, and in Japan the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry began its Study Group on Human Resource Policy in the Digital Age on 4 February 2021 and started to use the word as a term of policy.

The date it was handed to the public as a norm is 3 October 2022. In his policy speech, Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said that "investment in people", including public support for individual reskilling, would be expanded into a package of "one trillion yen over five years". It was among the 30 nominated words of the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award that year, but did not reach the top ten.

made.label: 2022 A policy speech
made.fact: The first meeting of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry's Study Group on Human Resource Policy in the Digital Age was on 4 February 2021. In his policy speech to the 210th session of the Diet on 3 October 2022, Prime Minister Fumio Kishida announced that the measures of "investment in people", including public support for individual reskilling, would be expanded into a package of "one trillion yen over five years". Nominated for the U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award that year.

keyfacts.text: At Davos in January 2020 the World Economic Forum launched the "Reskilling Revolution" (better skills for one billion people by 2030).

The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry's Study Group on Human Resource Policy in the Digital Age met first on 4 February 2021, then on 26 February, 11 March and 1 June, and published its report on 7 August 2023.

Prime Minister Kishida's policy speech (3 October 2022): on public support for individual reskilling, the measures of investment in people expanded into a package of "one trillion yen over five years". He announced that guidelines for smoothing labour mobility would be drawn up by June the following year.

"Reskilling" was a nominated word (one of 30) of the 2022 (39th) U-Can New Words and Buzzwords Award. The top ten were "Kyiv", "kitsune dance", "state funeral rite", "second-generation believers", "shiran kedo", "smartphone shoulder", "temaedori", "Yakult 1000" and "the bad weak yen"; the grand prize for the year was "Murakami-sama".

048.name: Edo Shigusa
048.hitokoto: Edo shigusa first appears in a newspaper column of 1981, in no Edo source at all.
body: Edo shigusa, known for kasa kashige, tilting the umbrella away, and kobushi koshi ukase, shifting along a bench by a fist's width, does not appear in a single line of any Edo-period source. The word first appears in a Yomiuri Shimbun column of 1981; its proponent Mitsuakira Shiba (real name Kazuo Kobayashi, 1928-1999) began to speak of it claiming descent from an "Edo-ko". His disciple Reiko Koshikawa put it into a book in 1992 as Edo no hanjo shigusa, and in a Kodansha Plus Alpha paperback of 2001 sold it as a merchant's code.

Koshikawa explained the absence of sources by saying that at the surrender of Edo Castle the new government's army massacred the Edokko who carried the tradition. The word spread all the same: the Japan Advertising Council used it in manners advertising for Tokyo in fiscal 2004 and fiscal 2005, an NPO was founded in 2007, and from fiscal 2014 it was handed to fifth- and sixth-year pupils across the country in the Ministry of Education's Watashitachi no dotoku, Our Morality.

In August 2014, when the historian Minoru Harada showed in Edo shigusa no shotai that it was an invention, Ikuhosha stopped printing it in its civics textbook from fiscal 2016. The ministry kept it in the revision of the same year, on the ground that "the material does not teach whether Edo shigusa is true or false". It is a specimen of what Hobsbawm called an invented tradition, set on the shelf with its date of manufacture attached.

made.label: 1981 The word first appears
made.fact: The first appearance in print of the words "Edo shigusa" is the Yomiuri Shimbun column "Henshu techo" of 1981. Its proponent Mitsuakira Shiba (real name Kazuo Kobayashi, 1928 - 22 January 1999) called himself a social education body, the "Society for Reconsidering the Good of Edo", and was taken up again in the Yomiuri column "Yomiuri sunpyo" of 23 March 1983. His disciple Reiko Koshikawa put it into a book as Edo no hanjo shigusa: this is how one became an Edokko (Nihon Keizai Shimbunsha, December 1992).

discontinued.label: 2014 Verified as false history
discontinued.fact: Minoru Harada's Edo shigusa no shotai: a false tradition eating away at education (Seikaisha Shinsho, 25 August 2014) pointed out that it does not appear in any Edo-period source at all. Criticism grew from 2015, and Ikuhosha, which had carried it in its civics textbook from fiscal 2012, stopped from fiscal 2016. The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, however, kept Edo shigusa in Watashitachi no dotoku: Elementary School Years 5 and 6 in the revision for fiscal 2016 as well.

keyfacts.text: Mitsuakira Shiba, real name Kazuo Kobayashi, also known as Taro Urashima, 1928 - 22 January 1999. He claimed to be a descendant of the head of an "Edo-ko" and said he had revived that Edo-ko in the Showa period as the "Society for Reconsidering the Good of Edo".

The first appearance in print of the words "Edo shigusa" is the Yomiuri Shimbun column "Henshu techo" of 1981. It was also introduced in the Yomiuri column "Yomiuri sunpyo" of 23 March 1983 (by Kiyoichi Murao).

Reiko Koshikawa's Edo no hanjo shigusa: this is how one became an Edokko is Nihon Keizai Shimbunsha, December 1992; Shonindo "Edo shigusa" no chiebukuro is Kodansha Plus Alpha Shinsho, September 2001.

In chapter seven of Shonindo "Edo shigusa" no chiebukuro, "The Edo shigusa that was wiped out", Koshikawa claims that at the surrender of Edo Castle the new government's army, fearing the "Edo-ko", massacred the Edokko who carried the tradition (an "Edokko hunt"), and that no sources survive for that reason.

The Japan Advertising Council (now AC Japan) made it an advertisement in its Tokyo regional campaign "Edo shigusa" for fiscal 2004 and "Edo shigusa, continued" for fiscal 2005 (illuminated boards, posters, internet advertising and so on; the theme for fiscal 2005 was "manners in Tokyo").

The NPO Edo Shigusa (now the NPO Nihon no Kokoro, Edo Shigusa) was certified by the Governor of Tokyo on 24 August 2007 and established on 5 September 2007 (registered as a corporation on 11 September). Its chair was Reiko Koshikawa.

"Edo shigusa" appears in the Ministry of Education's Watashitachi no dotoku: Elementary School Years 5 and 6 (distributed across the country from fiscal 2014). Ikuhosha adopted it in its civics textbook from fiscal 2012.

Minoru Harada's Edo shigusa no shotai: a false tradition eating away at education (Seikaisha Shinsho 52) was published on 25 August 2014: "Edo shigusa, contrary to its name, was produced in the 1980s by a defiant intellectual called Mitsuakira Shiba." The points of the criticism are that it appears in no Edo-period source at all; that kasa kashige does not fit how Japanese umbrellas were actually used; that toki dorobo, the time thief, contradicts the sense of time of the day; and that the massacre story of the "Edokko hunt" is preposterous. The sequel, Edo shigusa no shuen, is February 2016.

In April 2016 the ministry decided to keep Edo shigusa in the revision of Watashitachi no dotoku. The section chief responsible answered that "the moral education material does not teach whether Edo shigusa is true or false. The point is not whether it is right or wrong but to have pupils think about courtesy".
